42 Financial risk management objectives The Group’s activities expose it to market risk including foreign currency risk and interest rate risk, liquidity risk and credit risk. This note explains the sources of risk which the entity is exposed to and how the entity manages the risk : The Group’s risk management is carried out by a treasury department under policies approved by the Board of Directors. Treasury department identifies, evaluates and hedges financial risks in close co-operation with the Group’s operating units. The board provides principles for overall risk management, as well as policies covering specific areas, such as hedging of foreign currency transactions foreign exchange risk. (a) Market risk Market risk is the risk of any loss in future earnings, in realisable fair values or in future cash flows that may result from a change in the price of a financial instrument. The value of a financial instrument may change as result of changes in interest rates, foreign currency exchange rates, liquidity and other market changes. Future specific market movements can not be normally predicted with reasonable accuracy.
389 APL Apollo Tubes Limited Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the year ended March 31, 2025 (i) Foreign currency risk The Group’s functional currency (except for one subsidiary A P L Apollo Tubes Company L.L.C. incorporated in Dubai) in Indian Rupees (INR). The Group undertakes transactions denominated in the foreign currencies; consequently, exposure to exchange rate fluctuations arise. Volatility in exchange rates affects the Group’s revenue from export markets and the costs of imports, primarily in relation to import of capital goods. The Group is exposed to exchange rate risk under its trade and debt portfolio. Adverse movements in the exchange rate between the Rupee and any relevant foreign currency result’s in the increase in the Group’s overall debt positions in Rupee terms without the Group having incurred additional debt and favourable movements in the exchange rates will conversely result in reduction in the Group’s receivable in foreign currency. In order to hedge exchange rate risk, the Group has a policy to hedge cash flows up to a specific tenure using forward exchange contracts and options. At any point in time, the Group hedges its estimated foreign currency exposure in respect of forecast sales over the following 6 months or as deemed appropriate based on market conditions. In respect of imports and other payables, the Group hedges its payable as and when the exposure arises. The Group is exposed to interest rate risk because funds are borrowed at both fixed and floating interest rates. Interest rate risk is measured by using the cash flow sensitivity for changes in variable interest rate. The borrowings of the Group are principally denominated in rupees and US dollars with a mix of fixed and floating rates of interest. The Group hedges its US dollar interest rate risk through interest rate swaps to reduce the floating interest rate risk. The Group has exposure to interest rate risk, arising principally on changes in base lending rate. Recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments is provided for under Section 13 and Section 44A of the Civil Procedure Code (“Civil Code”) on a statutory basis. Section 44A of the Civil Code provides that where a foreign judgment has been rendered by a superior court, within the meaning of that Section, in any country or territory outside India which the Government has by notification declared to be in reciprocating territory, it may be enforced in India by proceedings in execution as if the judgment had been rendered by the relevant court in India. However, Section 44A of the Civil Code is applicable only to monetary decrees not being in the same nature of amounts payable in respect of taxes, other charges of a like nature or in respect of a fine or other penalties. The United Kingdom, Singapore and Hong Kong, among other countries, have been declared by the Government to be a reciprocating territory for the purposes of Section 44A of the Civil Procedure Code. A judgment of a court of a country which is not a reciprocating territory may be enforced in India only by a suit upon the judgment under Section 13 of the Civil Procedure Code, and not by proceedings in execution. Section 13 of the Civil Code provides that foreign judgments shall be conclusive regarding any matter directly adjudicated upon except: (i) where the judgment has not been pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction; (ii) where the judgment has not been given on the merits of the case; (iii) where it appears on the face of the proceedings that the judgment is founded on an incorrect view of international law or refusal to recognize the law of India in cases to which such law is applicable; (iv) where the proceedings in which the 63 judgment was obtained were opposed to natural justice; (v) where the judgment has been obtained by fraud; or (vi) where the judgment sustains a claim founded on a breach of any law then in force in India. Under the Civil Procedure Code, a court in India shall, upon the production of any document purporting to be a certified copy of a foreign judgment, presume that the judgment was pronounced by a court of competent jurisdiction, unless the contrary appears on record. Funding the working capital requirements of our Company; and We are focused on delivering end-to-end renewable energy solutions, including engineering, procurement and construction (“EPC”) of solar energy projects on a turnkey basis, with an emphasis on serving clients in the commercial and industrial sectors. We execute independent solar EPC projects for our clients. Under our model, we facilitate seamless project deployment from conceptualization and assisting in land acquisition to commissioning, and assist with obtaining the necessary approvals, including for evacuation lines from the solar power plant to the electricity grid on behalf of the clients. We provide our clients with customized solutions, which includes analysing the clients’ existing power consumption in comparison with the actual solar power generation that can be commissioned including options for the selection of suitable technologies available for commissioning of solar EPC Project. We execute independent solar EPC projects for our clients, wherein, our major business model involves the ground-mounted and roof top solar EPC Projects. We fund a majority of our working capital requirements in the ordinary course of business from borrowings and internal accruals. For details with respect to our Borrowings, see “Financial Indebtedness” on page 391. In 116 order to support the incremental business requirements, our Company requires additional working capital for funding its incremental working capital requirements in Fiscals 2027 and 2028. The funding of the incremental working capital requirements of our Company will lead to a consequent increase in our profitability and achieving the proposed targets as per our business plan. Requirement of Working capital As is inherent in the EPC contracting model, our working capital requirements are project-dependent and typically intensify with the scale, tenure and payment milestones associated with each contract. Each project typically requires both fund-based and non-fund-based banking facilities to meet its working capital requirements. Fund-based facilities provide the necessary cash flow to meet project-related operating and execution expenses, while non-fund-based facilities, such as bank guarantees and letters of credit, are required under the contractual and bid terms and are important for securing contracts and meeting the financial and performance requirements of our clients. In our projects, we are required to furnish bank guarantees to clients as part of the contractual terms. For securing such bank guarantees, we are required to provide cash margin and eligible collateral to our bankers, resulting in deployment and blockage of financial resources. Our working capital requirements are further influenced by milestone-based billing, retention clauses, delayed recoveries and extended payment cycles, as our projects are undertaken for government entities, either directly or indirectly, and payments are generally linked to contractual milestones, certification and other prescribed procedures. Rational for increase in working capital requirement: Earnest Money Deposits, Performance Bank Guarantees and Advance Payment Guarantees At the bidding stage, our Company is required to furnish Earnest Money Deposits (“EMDs”) or bid security for participation in tenders. The quantum and form of such bid security varies depending on the terms of the respective tender. The EMD is generally in the range of 1% to 2% of the quoted contract value/capacity and is required to remain valid during the prescribed bid validity period. Such amounts remain blocked during the bidding process and are generally refunded after approximately six months from the announcement of the bid results. Upon award of contracts, our Company is required to furnish Performance Bank Guarantees (“PBGs”) of approximately 2.5% to 5% of the contract value, depending on the nature and terms of the respective contract. Such guarantees generally remain valid during the project execution period of approximately 18 to 24 months and may, depending on the contractual terms, be extended to cover the defect liability period and other post-completion obligations. This results in utilization of our non-fund-based banking facilities and corresponding deployment of margin or collateral, thereby increasing our working capital requirements. Some of our clients provide advances of approximately 5% to 10% of the contract value towards mobilisation against which our Company is required to furnish a corresponding bank guarantee. Such arrangements require us to maintain adequate non-fund-based banking limits and collateral and consequently result in blockage of financial resources. Further, we may be required to provide collateral security for our non-fund-based and fund-based banking limits, including in the form of separate fixed deposits, resulting in further deployment of funds. Accordingly, with the increase in the number and value of projects undertaken by us, our requirement for EMDs, PBGs, ABGs and other bank guarantees also increases, resulting in higher deployment of working capital towards such contractual and banking requirements. Assumptions and Justifications of Holding Period Levels The working capital projections made by the Company are based on certain key assumptions and justifications, as set out below: 120 Particulars Details Trade Receivables Trade receivables represent amounts owed to the Company by its customers for the sale of goods and services in the ordinary course of business. Trade receivable days were 66 days, 87 days, and 181 days during Fiscal 2024, Fiscal 2025, and Fiscal 2026, respectively. The Company's trade receivables are primarily associated with government contracts and reflect the payment cycle dynamics inherent in the sector. These receivables also include retention money withheld by customers, which is generally released upon completion of the relevant projects, subject to fulfilment of applicable contractual conditions, thereby contributing to the overall receivable days. The increase in trade receivable days in Fiscal 2026 was also attributable to the increase in EPC revenue, which increased from ₹11,716.55 lakhs in Fiscal 2024 to ₹20,609.43 lakhs in Fiscal 2026, resulting in a corresponding increase in trade receivables. The receivable cycle is also influenced by the nature and complexity of project execution, including administrative delays, pending departmental clearances, approvals, project milestone certifications and other contractual requirements before billing and collection. The increase in trade receivables projected for Fiscal 2027 and Fiscal 2028 is primarily attributable to the anticipated scaling up of business operations and revenue, supported by the Company's order book. Accordingly, trade receivable days are projected at 147 days and 146 days during Fiscal 2027 and Fiscal 2028, respectively. Inventories Our inventory primarily comprises work-in-progress (“WIP”) arising from our EPC projects. Given our business model and milestone-based billing arrangements, inventory holding periods were 78 days, 119 days and 101 days during Fiscal 2024, Fiscal 2025 and Fiscal 2026, respectively. The level of inventory is influenced by the long execution cycles of our EPC projects, which require materials and WIP to be maintained at various stages of project execution. With the anticipated increase in revenue from ongoing projects as of March 31, 2026 and new projects awarded during Fiscal 2027, we expect inventory to increase in absolute terms. However, the inventory holding period is expected to remain broadly aligned with the requirements of our ongoing project execution. Accordingly, the inventory holding period is projected at 101 days and is expected to stabilize at 100 days from Fiscal 2028 onwards. The IMF forecasts GDP growth for India at 6.40% in CY26, far outpacing the estimated CY26 global average of 3.00%. This performance reflects a combination of strong domestic fundamentals, policy stability and a sustained focus on capital formation. While the global economy continues to face uncertainty from geopolitical conflicts, commodity price volatility and rising public debt, India’s diversified growth drivers, stable policy framework and expanding export ecosystem position it well to navigate these headwinds. The key sectors with potential exposure to changes in US tariff policy include engineering goods, electronics, gems and jewellery, pharmaceuticals, textiles and automobiles/auto components, given their material export linkages to the US market. As of August 2026, the US-India trade relationship faces renewed uncertainty. The US Senate has passed the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which could allow the US President to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from major buyers of Russian energy, including India. The bill is not itself a 100% tariff currently in force, but it creates a significant additional risk for Indian exporters if enacted and applied. In July 2026, the US had imposed a baseline tariff of 10% on roughly 70% of Indian manufactured exported goods (covering textiles, engineering items, gems, and machinery. India continues to strengthen its position through diversification of trade partnerships and expansion of FTAs with the European Union, the United Kingdom, EFTA and other key economies. India further continues to strengthen its position through diversification of trade partnerships and expansion of FTAs. The India-UK Free Trade Agreement officially came into effect on 15th July 2026, providing improved market access and lower trade barriers between the two countries. The agreement is expected to support greater trade in goods and services and create new opportunities for Indian exporters. India is also continuing engagement with the EU, EFTA, GCC and other key markets to reduce dependence on any single trading partner. The US-Iran conflict remains ongoing and uncertainties around the same remain. As of August 2026, negotiations have stalled, with the US stating that no formal talks are currently planned with Iran. The Iran conflict has led to an increase in prices of consumer products in India due to potentially higher fuel, freight and input costs, which can make everyday goods like FMCG items, plastics and packaged foods more expensive. Disruptions in shipping and fertiliser supplies are also pushing up food prices, affecting imports of agricultural inputs and leading to costlier food products for consumers. Overall, delays in trade routes and rising logistics costs are reducing availability and increasing prices of imported consumer goods, especially from Gulf-linked supply chains. Overall, this is leading to supply shortages, rising costs, and production slowdowns in India’s chemical and pharma sectors, with the impact likely to worsen if the conflict continues. Prolonged geopolitical tensions or conflict in the region could lead to sustained increases in crude oil and LPG prices, which may translate into higher input costs across industries and contribute to inflationary pressures in the Indian economy. Policy momentum remains strong. The 56th meeting of the GST Council marked a major structural reform by proposing a simplified two-rate system of 5% and 18%, replacing the earlier four-slab framework, along with a 152 40% demerit rate for luxury and sin goods. This rationalisation aims to reduce compliance burdens, enhance efficiency, and stimulate private consumption. Improving rural demand, supported by healthy monsoon progress, favourable sowing conditions, and adequate reservoir levels, provides additional tailwinds for consumption and investment. 2 Indian Power Sector 2.1 Overview Of The Indian Power Sector India’s power sector reforms have progressively transformed the electricity industry from a vertically integrated, state-controlled model to a more competitive and market-oriented framework. Key milestones include the opening of generation to private participation in the 1990s, the establishment of independent regulatory commissions through the Electricity Regulatory Commissions Act, 1998, and the enactment of the Electricity Act, 2003, which introduced competition, open access, and structural unbundling across the value chain. The structure of the power industry is depicted in the figure below: The power industry is divided into three core segments • Generation - Production of electricity from fossil and non-fossil fuel-based sources like solar and wind. • Transmission - Enables the bulk transfer of electricity from power plants to distribution substations through a high-voltage network. • Distribution - Retail electricity distribution involves supply of electricity to consumers at lower voltage levels. India’s power and renewable energy sector is governed by the Ministry of Power (MoP) and the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), which serve as nodal ministries responsible for policy formulation and sectoral development. Regulatory oversight is provided by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) and State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs), which are independent statutory Electricity Regulatory Authorities that are responsible for tariff regulation, licensing, market development, consumer protection, and renewable energy promotion. The Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI), a Navratna PSU under MNRE, plays a key role in advancing renewable energy deployment. It facilitates the development of solar, wind and hybrid projects, and acts as an intermediary between renewable energy developers and distribution companies through Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) and Power Sale Agreements (PSAs). 2.2 Operating and Regulatory Structure India’s power sector has undergone a gradual transformation from a state-controlled electricity system to a competitive and market-oriented framework. This evolution has been driven by successive policy reforms, institutional strengthening, and the introduction of independent regulatory mechanisms that support sector growth and private participation. Fiscal and regulatory incentives Mandatory renewable procurement targets have created a stable demand base for renewable energy across states and obligated entities.
Renewable purchase obligation Initiatives such as Green Energy Corridors, transmission expansion and grid modernisation have strengthened renewable energy evacuation and integration.
Infrastructure support from government Growing demand for cost savings and sustainability commitments has increased renewable energy adoption among commercial and industrial consumers.
Traction in C&I segment The introduction of dedicated renewable energy trading platforms has enhanced market liquidity and enabled flexible power procurement.
Green-Term ahead market Renewable projects generally have shorter gestation periods, lower operating costs and limited fuel price exposure compared to conventional power plants.

Such infrastructure may include developed land, internal roads, power evacuation and transmission facilities, water supply and other common utilities and amenities, thereby enabling solar power developers to establish and operate their projects in a more efficient and coordinated manner. Generally, the capacity of solar parks is 500 MW and above. However, due to a shortage of non-agricultural land, smaller parks that are up to 20 MW are also considered in states and union territories. Around 4 to 5 acres of land is required for setting up solar parks. Schemes for Development of Solar Parks In December 2014, the Government of India introduced the Scheme for the Development of Solar Parks and Ultra-Mega Solar Power Projects, initially aiming for a capacity of 20,000 MW. This target was later raised to 40,000 MW in March 2017, with the goal of establishing at least 50 solar parks. The scheme is set to continue until 31 March 2026. The Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) and the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA) are tasked with implementing the scheme and managing its funds on behalf of the government. Under the schemes, central financial assistance (CFA) of up to Rs 25 lakhs per solar park is provided for preparation of detailed project report (DPR). Along with this, CFA of Rs 20 lakh per MW or 30% of the project cost, whichever is lower, is also provided on achieving the milestones prescribed in the scheme. The total grant approved under the scheme is Rs 8,100 crores. Approved and Established Solar Parks The government under its Development of Solar Parks and Ultra Mega Solar Power Projects scheme has targeted a cumulative installation of 40 GW of large-scale, grid-connected solar power plants. Under this initiative, 56 solar parks with an aggregate capacity of 42,107 MW have been approved across 12 states. As of CEA June 2026, 23 solar parks, with an aggregate capacity of approximately 14,491 MW, have been fully developed, with around 14,066 MW of operational solar projects within these parks. Additionally, solar projects have been commissioned in several other solar parks which are still under various stages of development. Together, 21,312 MW of solar projects have already been commissioned across Solar Parks/UMREPPs in the 169 country, while 9,065 MW is currently under construction and 11,155 MW is under the award/tendering process. Out of the total envisaged capacity of 42,107 MW, 30,657 MW has been awarded, which includes 21,312 MW that has already been commissioned and 9,065 MW currently under construction. In FY25, a total Central Financial Assistance of around Rs 163.6 Crore has been released to various Park Developers/CTU/STU under the scheme. Technical Factors to Hinder Growth in Rooftop Solar Capacity Additions Despite the favourable policy environment, rooftop solar deployment continues to face several structural challenges. Its objective is to increase farmers' income while offering options for irrigation and reducing diesel dependency in the agricultural sector. The primary goal of PM KUSUM is to ensure energy security for farmers in India, while fulfilling India’s commitment to increase the proportion of installed electric power capacity from non-fossil-fuel sources to 40% by 2030, as part of its Intended Nationally Determined Contributions (INDCs). The scheme aims to increase solar capacity by 34,800 MW, with a total central financial support of Rs 344.22 billion. The scheme was approved by the Cabinet Committee on 19th February, 2019, and consists of 3 components: During 2024, • Component A: 10,000 MW of decentralised, ground-mounted, grid-connected solar power plants. • Component B: Installation of 20 lakh standalone solar-powered agriculture pumps. • Component C: Solarisation of 15 lakh existing grid-connected agriculture pumps. All components combined would support the installation of additional solar capacity of 34.80 GW. As of July 2026, 1,986.30 MW of solar capacity has been installed under Component A against the sanctioned capacity of 10,000 MW, representing 19.9% achievement. Under Component B, 11,68,667 standalone solar-powered agricultural pumps have been installed against 13,07,190 sanctioned pumps, representing 89.4% achievement. Under Component C, 16,259 individual grid-connected agricultural pumps have been solarised under Individual Pump Solarisation (IPS) against 55,392 sanctioned pumps, representing 29.4% achievement. Further, under Feeder Level Solarisation (FLS), 35,36,602 agricultural pumps have been sanctioned, of which 46.8% have been solarised. The PM-KUSUM scheme has been extended up to 31st March 2027 to facilitate completion of the sanctioned projects. 3.8.2. EPC services can be classified into various subcategories based on the scale and type of installations, i.e., Utility Scale Solar, rooftop solar and Distributed/Off-grid solar installations. Favourable government initiatives, such as MNRE’s target of achieving 280 GW of solar energy capacity by fiscal year 2030, have led to a sharp rise in ground-mounted utility-scale solar installations, accounting for the majority of India’s solar capacity. In parallel, increased demand for green energy and rooftop installations by corporate consumers have also boosted solar installations. However, the Solar EPC sector in India presents high entry barriers, as it demands a minimum level of technical expertise and experience to qualify for tenders, along with restrictions on joint ventures participating in bids. Solar EPC projects are generally executed through separate supply and services contracts rather than a single EPC 179 arrangement. High-value equipment such as modules, inverters, transformers and cables, which together account for about 70–75% of project cost, is usually sourced directly by developers. Execution-related activities, including civil works, installation and commissioning, form the balance 25–30% of costs and are assigned to specialised service contractors. In certain cases, solar module manufacturers also undertake full EPC responsibilities, covering both supply and project execution. Solar EPC contracts vary based on the assignment of roles and responsibilities and penalties. Based on these differences, various project delivery mechanisms have been devised. The size and nature of the project also influence the choice of the project delivery mechanism. 4.1 Market Size of Solar EPC India’s installed solar capacity is rising rapidly, supported by MNRE’s plan to invite ~50 GW of renewable bids annually from FY24–FY28 to achieve 500 GW by 2030. The contractor is then solely responsible for completing the project and handing it over to the owner in a turnkey project condition. The EPC phase of a project is called as the 17.4 185-195 FY25 FY26-32E GWAC 180 execution phase, which is after the feasibility study and front-end engineering design study phase. But some EPC players also do feasibility studies to participate in tenders. The Key Features of an EPC contract are as follows: • Single point ownership and responsibility • Clearly defined deliverables and project specifications • Fixed completion date • Fixed completion price • Procurement responsibilities • Output Guarantees • Liquidated damages to the client company for both delay and performance • Security from the contractor or its parent company • Caps on liability Solar EPC contracts vary based on assignment of roles and responsibilities and penalty. Based on these differences, various project delivery mechanisms have been devised. The size and nature of the project also influence the choice of the project delivery mechanism. EPC Project: Turnkey vs Balance of Plant There are two types of modes for the EPC contract to be executed – the turnkey project structure and balance of plant structure. Under the turnkey project structure, the EPC company/contractor takes care of everything from design to execution of the work, which includes EPC. The contractor delivers ready-to-use facilities. The project must be completed within an agreed-upon budget and schedule. If these conditions are not met, the contractor may need to offer financial compensation. The turnkey solar project consists of the following process- Survey of the site to check solar viability - The location of the project is surveyed to determine the future weather forecast and solar isolation. Determination of solar power generation capacity and connection type - Solar PV installations can be made in grid-connection or off-grid connection types depending on the installation capacity and consumption pattern of the client. The solar companies would determine the power generation capacity by considering the structure of the terrain and the amount of incident sunlight. Engineering and design of solar PV system - While designing and engineering of the solar panels, angle, height, weather, roof structure, etc. are considered. The mounting structure for the solar array is constructed according to approved design and study. Solar Power Plant Installation - After carefully considering all the project requirements, the panels are carefully installed. Metering of Solar Power Plant- A turnkey solution provider considers factors such as electricity tariffs, power output and usage to prepare a net metering agreement that best suits your needs. Solar Financing Solutions and Approvals- The turnkey solution providers might also have tie-ups with the financing organizations, private investors, etc., whenever required by the client. Monitoring of Solar Panel Efficiency- The efficiency of solar PV modules is due to depreciation over a longer period. The solar turnkey solution providers monitor the efficiency of the panels and maintain the uniform 181 efficiency of the panels by taking care of their sub-parts. Operation and Maintenance- After the installation of the solar panels, it requires occasional cleaning and is performed by the turnkey solution providers. They also manage the operations of the installed equipment and accessories. Under the balance of plant (BoP) or the balance of system (BoS) structure, the entire project is divided into different parts. Generally, the modules, which form majority of the cost of the solar plant, are procured separately by the developer and the remaining segments including wiring, switches, mounting system, inverters, batteries etc. are procured under the EPC contract along with the project installation services Third Party EPC Contracts - refers to an agreements where a solar project developer or investor outsources the complete responsibility of Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) to an external contractor instead of executing the project in-house. This model is widely adopted in utility-scale and increasingly in commercial & industrial (C&I) solar projects, where developers seek efficiency, speed, and technical expertise. This type of contracts provides flexibility in terms of risk mitigation, access to expertise, cost and time efficiency, quality assurance. The full lifecycle of project execution is managed by them, including site survey, design and engineering, procurement of modules, inverters, and balance-of-system components, installation, commissioning, and O&M support. As India accelerates toward its renewable energy targets, the demand for professional EPC services is rising. Many investors, IPPs (Independent Power Producers), and C&I customers prefer third-party EPC models to avoid the capital intensity of building in-house execution capabilities. 4.3 Key Covenants of an EPC Contract The EPC contract is established between the client (the owner) and the EPC contractor for a specific project or scope that the contractor is obligated to deliver Client Scoping Clearly specifies technical standards, performance criteria and deliverables. The transmission network facilitates long-distance bulk transfer of electricity from generating stations to load centres through high-voltage networks, while the distribution system delivers electricity from substations to residential, commercial, industrial and agricultural consumers at lower voltage levels. India's T&D network has expanded significantly over the past decade in line with rising electricity demand, universal electrification and increasing renewable energy capacity additions. State-owned distribution companies (DISCOMs) primarily oversee this process. Moreover, distribution franchises have played a significant role in reducing distribution losses in the areas they serve. In cities like Delhi, Surat, Ahmedabad, Kolkata and Mumbai, private licenses have been granted distribution rights and have demonstrated efficient operations. The consumer base of DISCOMs is made up of five main segments: domestic, commercial, agricultural, industrial and others. The improvement in recovery of outstanding dues has been due to the implementation of Electricity (Late Payment Surcharge and Related Matters) Rules, 2022, which were notified in August 2022. The rules were introduced to strengthen the regulatory provisions for recovery of outstanding dues of generating, transmission and electricity trading licenses from distribution companies. The rules include late payment surcharge, prior intimation of payment schedule, priority-wise adjustment of payment and EMI schedule structure. Further, under these rules, it has become difficult for DISCOMs to access power after the trigger date or in case of payment defaults unless the dues are settled. The DISCOMs are now given forty-five days by the power producers to pay bills towards electricity supplied, after which the outstanding dues become overdue and the DISCOMs are penalised in most cases. Delay in payments by the DISCOMs adversely affect the cash flows of the generating companies, and hence, the generating companies need to make provisions for purchasing inputs like coal and keep adequate working capital. This impacts the entire value chain of the power sector. Schemes like the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) have been introduced to improve the operational efficiency and financial sustainability of DISCOMs. The government is now seeking a 2-year extension of the RDSS scheme until FY28 to accelerate smart-meter rollouts and strengthen distribution infrastructure. This sector relies on a complex grid of transmission lines, substations, and transformers that link power plants to load centres. This interconnected grid ensures that if a local generator fails or a line is out for maintenance, electricity can be rerouted to prevent outages. 196 In India, the transmission and distribution (T&D) network follows a three-level hierarchy The system operates across four primary voltage categories as mentioned above EHV, HV, MV and LV The electricity supply system in India operates across a hierarchy of standardised voltage levels to ensure efficient transmission, reliable distribution, and safe end-use consumption of power. Extra High Voltage (EHV) levels, including 220 kV, 400 kV, and 765 kV (along with ±500 kV and ±800 kV HVDC systems), are primarily used for long-distance bulk power transmission from generation sources to major load centres, inter-state transmission networks and renewable energy evacuation corridors, as higher voltages significantly reduce transmission losses. Power received at EHV substations is stepped down to High Voltage (HV) levels such as 66 kV, 110 kV, and 132 kV, which serve as sub-transmission networks supplying power to urban load centres, large industrial consumers, traction systems, and primary distribution substations. From there, electricity is further stepped down to Medium Voltage (MV) levels of 33 kV, 22 kV, and 11 kV for primary distribution within cities, towns, industrial estates, and rural areas, forming the key part of the distribution network. Finally, power is delivered to end-consumers at Low Voltage (LV) levels, typically 415 V for three-phase and 230 V for single-phase supply, catering to residential households, small commercial establishments and public infrastructure such as street lighting. This standardised voltage framework enables optimal system efficiency, equipment interoperability, grid stability, and safe electricity delivery across the entire power sector value chain. 6.6 Impact of Government Power Policy on T&D Infrastructure Over the past decade, India's power transmission and distribution infrastructure has transformed considerably. This evolution was primarily driven by strategic policy initiatives focused on several key areas: expanding grid capacity, boosting system reliability, integrating renewable energy sources and improving the financial stability of utility companies. These collective efforts have successfully channelled substantial capital investment, extended the reach of the power network, and enhanced the overall operational efficiency throughout the entire T&D value chain. 1. National Electricity Policy (NEP) and Electricity Act Framework The National Electricity Policy and the Electricity Act, 2003 provide the overarching regulatory and policy framework for the power sector. These policies emphasise non-discriminatory open access, development of a robust national grid, and promotion of competition and private sector participation. As a result, transmission planning has shifted towards creating a strong inter-regional and inter-state transmission network, enabling seamless power flow across regions and optimal utilisation of generation capacity. The policy framework has also encouraged standardisation of grid codes, technical norms, and planning criteria, thereby improving system stability and long-term network resilience. 2. Renewable Energy Policies and Green Energy Corridors India’s aggressive renewable energy targets of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030 are having a transformative impact on transmission infrastructure. Policies promoting large-scale solar and wind development have necessitated the creation of dedicated renewable energy evacuation systems, including Green Energy Corridors and high-capacity interstate transmission systems (ISTS). These initiatives have driven investments in extra-high voltage (EHV) AC and HVDC lines, pooling substations, and advanced grid management systems to handle intermittency. Consequently, transmission planning has become more forward-looking, focused on integrating geographically dispersed renewable resources with major demand centres. 197 3. Tariff-based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) Guidelines The introduction of tariff-based competitive bidding for transmission projects has significantly altered the sector’s execution landscape. Under TBCB, private developers compete to build and operate transmission assets at the lowest discovered tariff, improving cost efficiency and accelerating project timelines. This policy has increased private sector participation, reduced dependence on public funding, and introduced global best practices in project execution, risk management, and asset operation. The resulting competitive environment has contributed to faster expansion of transmission capacity and more disciplined capital deployment. 4. Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) The RDSS focuses on improving the operational and financial performance of distribution companies through targeted investments in infrastructure and technology. Key components include feeder segregation, system strengthening, underground cabling in urban areas, deployment of smart prepaid meters, and modernisation of substations. By reducing technical and commercial losses and improving billing and collection efficiency, RDSS indirectly strengthens the transmission segment as well, as financially healthier DISCOMs are better positioned to support grid expansion and honour transmission charges. The scheme also supports enhanced load forecasting and network planning at the distribution level. 5. Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) Rules, 2022 The LPS Rules were introduced to address chronic payment delays by DISCOMs to generators and transmission utilities. By mandating timely payments, restructuring legacy dues into fixed instalments, and linking access to scheduling with payment compliance, these rules have improved cash flow visibility and payment security across the sector. Improved financial discipline has reduced counterparty risk for transmission utilities and EPC players, enabling smoother project execution and encouraging continued investment in transmission infrastructure. 6. Integrated Transmission Planning and National Grid Initiatives Policy emphasis on integrated generation and transmission planning, led by agencies such as the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), has resulted in coordinated development of transmission networks aligned with future demand and capacity additions. National Grid initiatives have strengthened inter-regional connectivity, enhanced transfer capability, and improved system reliability. This integrated approach has minimised congestion risks, reduced regional imbalances, and enabled efficient power markets. 6.7 Overview of RDSS (Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme) 6.7.1 Outlay Launched in July 2021 with an outlay of Rs 3.04 trillion, including Gross Budgetary Support of Rs 976.3 billion, the RDSS is a reforms-based and results-linked scheme aimed at improving the operational efficiency and financial sustainability of power distribution utilities. The scheme provides financial support primarily for prepaid smart metering, system metering and upgradation of distribution infrastructure. It aims to reduce pan-India AT&C losses to 12-15% and eliminate the ACS-ARR gap. 6.7.2 Scope The RDSS focuses on modernizing power distribution networks through replacement of old conductors, augmentation and creation of substations and Distribution Transformers (DTs), feeder segregation, smart metering and implementation of SCADA/DMS systems. As of August 2026, around Rs 2.84 trillion of works had been sanctioned under the scheme, comprising Rs 1.53 trillion for loss-reduction infrastructure and Rs 1.31 trillion for smart metering. Cumulative funds released under RDSS since FY23 stood at Rs 471.24 billion as of August 2026. 6.7.3 State-wise Rollout Status Prepaid smart metering remains one of the key components of RDSS, aimed at improving billing and collection efficiency, energy accounting and the financial sustainability of DISCOMs. Smart metering works have been sanctioned across 28 States and 45 distribution utilities, covering 19.79 crore consumer meters, 52.53 lakh Distribution Transformer meters and 2.05 lakh feeder meters, aggregating to around 20.33 crore smart meters. The pace of RDSS implementation has accelerated, with cumulative smart meter installations increasing by 1.83 crore meters within six months, reaching 5.73 crore as of June 2026 against the sanctioned target of 19.8 crore meters. Overall smart meter installations in India, including installations under State plans and other schemes, 198 reached 7.24 crore by August 2026. RDSS funding deployment remains concentrated in a few large states, with Uttar Pradesh (Rs 15,989 crore), Rajasthan (Rs 12,688 crore), Maharashtra (Rs 12,673 crore), and Tamil Nadu (Rs 8,659 crore) emerging as the largest beneficiaries of sanctioned Gross Budgetary Support (GBS). While the national progress of loss reduction works stood at 42.2%, states such as West Bengal (65.5%), Assam (61.5%), Tripura (59.3%), and Jharkhand (59.2%) have emerged as frontrunners, showing stronger on-ground execution despite comparatively lower funding allocations. The allocation pattern indicates a strong focus on infrastructure strengthening and loss reduction, with the majority of sanctioned funding directed toward states having large distribution networks and significant efficiency improvement potential. 6.8 Rural Electrification Schemes The Government of India, working along with the State Governments, has achieved electrification of all inhabited unelectrified census villages and all willing households identified under flagship programmes such as Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY) and Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (SAUBHAGYA). According to the United Nations (2023), 64% of its population resides in rural areas, while the remaining 36% is concentrated in urban centres. India has a challenge of serving 18% of the world population with 4% of the world’s freshwater resources. Currently, India stores less than one-tenth of the annual rainfall and is designated to be a water-stressed nation. Disproportionate use of water for agricultural use, excessive groundwater pumping and deficient monsoon in the last couple of years make the demand-supply balance more critical. India is facing water crisis with around 50% of the population experiencing high-to-extreme water shortage, as per NITI Aayog. Annual per capita water availability is largely determined by regional hydro-meteorological and geological factors. With a steadily rising population, India’s per capita water availability has been declining. As per the “Reassessment of Water Availability in India using Space Inputs (2019),” the annual per capita availability has fallen below 1,700 cubic metres and is projected to decline further to 1,367 cubic metres by 2031. The Dynamic Ground Water Resource Assessment 2024 reports that of the 6,746 assessed units including blocks, talukas, mandals, watersheds, and firkas 751 units (11.13%) have been classified as ‘over-exploited’. It is expected that by 2050, about 1,450 km3 of water will be required out of which approximately 75% will be used in agriculture, ~7% for drinking water, ~4% in industries, ~9% for energy generation. Key Focus Areas: Rural Areas: Expansion of piped drinking-water infrastructure, including water treatment, bulk water transmission, distribution networks, storage facilities, household tap connections and greywater management. It aims to ensure piped water access to every household in rural India. The initiative was launched on 15 August 2019 by the Prime Minister of India. The programme is implemented in partnership with States to ensure tap water supply in adequate quantity, prescribed quality, adequate pressure, on a regular and long-term basis in all rural households and public institutions, which includes anganwadi, schools, ashramshalas, public/ community health centres, sub-centres, wellness centres, community centres, gram panchayat buildings, etc., by the year 2024. Under JJM, 30% weightage was assigned for difficult terrains, which include areas under Desert Development Programme (DDP) and Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP) while allocating the fund, to prioritise the coverage in these areas. Further, provisions have been made in the operational guidelines for planning and implementation of bulk water transfer from long distances and regional water supply schemes for ensuring tap water supply in drought-prone & water-scarce areas/ areas with inadequate rainfall or dependable groundwater sources. In addition, provisions have also been made for source recharging, viz. dedicated bore well recharge structures, rain water recharge, rejuvenation of existing water bodies, etc., in convergence with other schemes such as the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 (MGNREGA), Integrated Watershed Management Programme (IWMP), 15th Finance Commission tied grants to Rural Local Bodies (RLB)/ Panchayat Raj Institutions (PRI), State schemes, Corporate Social Responsibility funds, etc. For villages in water-scarce areas, in order to save the precious fresh water, states are also being encouraged to plan new water supply schemes with dual piped water supply system, i.e. supply of fresh water in one and treated grey/ wastewater in another pipe for non-potable/ gardening/ toilet flushing use. Moreover, the households in these areas are to be encouraged to use faucet aerators that save a significant amount of water, in multiple taps that they may be using inside their house. Conductors are manufactured using materials with high electrical conductivity, aluminium and copper being the primary materials used across power infrastructure applications. Aluminium is widely used in overhead transmission and distribution lines due to its relatively lower weight and cost compared with copper, while copper is commonly used in applications requiring higher electrical conductivity and compact conductor dimensions. In power transmission and distribution systems, conductors are used to carry electricity from generating stations to substations and subsequently to consumers. Overhead transmission and distribution lines generally use stranded conductors, wherein multiple wires are helically stranded together to provide the required combination of electrical conductivity, mechanical strength, flexibility and dimensional characteristics. Aluminium conductors, including Aluminium Conductor Steel Reinforced (ACSR), All Aluminium Alloy Conductor (AAAC) and All Aluminium Conductor (AAC), are among the commonly used conductors in India's transmission and distribution network. 211 India's requirement for electrical conductors is linked to the expansion and modernisation of its transmission and distribution infrastructure, increasing electricity demand, renewable energy integration, replacement and augmentation of existing networks and distribution-system strengthening. As per the IEEMA’s % Growth index for Electrical Equipment Industry conductors grew at 2.1% in FY24 vis-à-vis 18.4% in FY26 recording more than 8x growth. CareEdge estimates the market for electrical conductors to be between Rs 225-230 billion in FY26, the same is expected to grow at a CAGR of 4 to 5% in next 5 years. 8.4.1 Types and Application of Electrical Conductors Types Description Application AAC – All Aluminium Conductor AAC consists of stranded aluminium wires and does not contain a separate reinforcing core. It offers high electrical conductivity and is relatively lightweight. However, its mechanical strength is lower than that of conductors incorporating a steel or high-strength core. Used in distribution networks, substations and electrical connections. AAAC – All Aluminium Alloy Conductor AAAC is manufactured using aluminium alloy wires, generally providing higher mechanical strength than conventional AAC while maintaining aluminium-based construction. Its alloy composition provides improved mechanical and corrosion characteristics compared with conventional aluminium conductors. Used in overhead transmission and distribution networks, ACSR –Aluminium Condu ctor Steel Reinforced ACSR comprises aluminium wires stranded around a galvanised steel core. The aluminium provides electrical conductivity while the steel core provides mechanical strength and enables longer spans. It is one of the commonly used conductors for overhead transmission and distribution lines in India. Used in overhead transmission and distribution lines across different voltage levels. ACSR-type/ aluminium alloy reinforced conductors These conductors combine aluminium or aluminium alloy conducting layers with a reinforcing core to provide a balance between electrical and mechanical characteristics. Variants include AACSR and other alloy-reinforced configurations. Used in transmission and distribution systems where a specific configuration is selected based on voltage, span, loading and environmental requirements. HTLS – High Temperature Low Sag Conductors HTLS conductors are high-performance conductors designed to operate at higher temperatures while maintaining lower thermal elongation and sag compared with conventional conductors. Their characteristics enable higher power transfer through existing or constrained transmission corridors. Used for uprating existing transmission lines, increasing power-transfer capability within existing rights-of-way and for new transmission lines where higher current-carrying capacity is required. Copper Conductors Copper has higher electrical conductivity than aluminium and can provide high current-carrying capacity within a comparatively smaller cross-sectional area. However, it is heavier and generally has a higher material cost. Used in electrical equipment, substations, industrial electrical systems, building wiring, earthing and other applications where higher conductivity or compact dimensions are required. Covered / insulated conductors These comprise a conducting element with an insulating or protective covering. Unlike conventional bare overhead conductors, the covering provides additional protection against accidental contact and Used in distribution networks, particularly in areas with vegetation, constrained clearances, dense urban development or higher risk of accidental contact. 212 environmental conditions. 8.5 Key Demand Drivers 8.6 Key Challenges • Volatile Raw Material Costs The sector is heavily reliant on critical inputs such as copper, aluminium, and PVC, which together account for a significant share of production expenses. Fluctuations in global commodity prices directly affect profitability and create uncertainty in pricing strategies. Given the competitive nature of the market, transferring these cost increases to end- users is often difficult, resulting in sustained margin pressure. • Competitive Intensity And Pricing Stress India’s wires and cables market reflects a divided structure, with recognised brands facing competition from numerous unorganised players. The latter often undercuts prices aggressively, forcing established manufacturers to balance competitive pricing with quality, compliance, and service standards. This dynamic compresses margins and intensifies rivalry across the sector. • Import Reliance for Specialised Inputs While India has built a strong domestic base for conventional wires and cables, specialised products, advanced insulation materials, and high-end technology components are still largely imported. This reliance exposes the industry to risks such as supply chain disruptions, currency volatility, and changes in import duties, particularly during periods of geopolitical instability. • Quality Risks from Unorganised Players The widespread availability of low-cost, substandard products in the unorganised market remains a persistent challenge. These products often fail to meet safety and performance standards, increasing the risk of electrical hazards and eroding consumer confidence. For organised players, differentiating themselves purely on quality becomes difficult in such an environment. • Delays in Infrastructure and Power Projects A significant portion of demand for wires and cables is tied to infrastructure, construction, and power transmission projects. Delays caused by land acquisition hurdles, regulatory approvals, or funding constraints can directly affect order flows and revenue visibility for manufacturers, creating uncertainty in demand planning. • High Working Capital Intensity 213 The industry requires substantial working capital due to inventory holding of raw materials, extended receivable cycles, and project-based execution models. Manufacturers often need to maintain adequate stock levels to manage raw material price swings and ensure timely delivery, which places financial strain on small and mid-sized players. • Evolving Technology and Product Innovation Needs The growing adoption of smart grids, renewable energy systems, electric vehicles, and advanced communication infrastructure has increased demand for specialised and technologically advanced cables. Continuous investment in product innovation, testing, and R&D is essential to remain competitive, but smaller firms often struggle to keep pace with these requirements. • Compliance with Regulatory and Safety Norms The sector operates under stringent quality and safety standards set by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and other regulatory authorities. Compliance requires regular testing, certifications, and adherence to technical specifications. While these regulations enhance product reliability, they also raise compliance costs and add operational complexity, particularly for smaller manufacturers. • Rising Logistics and Operational Expenses Transportation costs, fuel price volatility, and supply chain inefficiencies significantly affect the cost structure of wires and cables manufacturers. Given the bulky nature of these products and the need for large-scale distribution, logistics expenses form a critical component of overall costs, impacting operational efficiency and profitability. 8.7 Key Government Policies/Regulations The Indian wires and cables industry is closely linked to the country’s infrastructure, power, industrial, and telecom sectors, making government policies and regulations a key growth enabler for the industry. Over the years, the Government of India has introduced several initiatives aimed at improving electrification, strengthening transmission infrastructure, promoting renewable energy, and encouraging domestic manufacturing. These policies have significantly supported demand generation while also improving product quality, safety standards, and localisation of manufacturing. 214 8.8 Tailwinds Supporting Sustainable Growth 1.Infrastructure-led Demand Environment Remains Active India’s infrastructure spending continues to provide a demand base for wires and cables across power, construction, transportation, urban infrastructure, and industrial projects. Public capital expenditure increased from Rs 2 lakh crore in FY15 to a Budget Estimate of Rs 12.2 lakh crore in FY27, indicating continued emphasis on asset creation and infrastructure development. For the wires and cables industry, this supports demand across building wires, low-voltage cables, medium-voltage cables, control cables, instrumentation cables, and speciality cables used in public infrastructure, utilities, industrial facilities, and urban projects. 2. Expansion of Power Transmission Network Power transmission remains one of the key end-use segments for the wires and cables industry. India’s transmission network crossed 5 lakh circuit kilometres of transmission lines at 220 kV and above, along with 1,407 GVA of transformation capacity, as of January 2026. Ongoing transmission projects are expected to add approximately 40,000 circuit kilometres of inter-state transmission lines and 27,500 circuit kilometres of intra-state transmission lines. This development is directly relevant to demand for high-voltage cables, conductors, power cables, control cables, and substation-related cabling solutions. 3. Renewable Energy Capacity Addition Supporting Specialised Cable Demand Renewable energy expansion continues to influence cable demand, particularly for solar cables, wind-energy 215 cables, evacuation infrastructure, underground cabling, and grid-connection systems. As of 31 May 2026, India’s total renewable energy capacity stood at 282.75 GW, while total non-fossil capacity stood at 291.53 GW. Within this, solar power accounted for 157.05 GW, wind power accounted for 56.81 GW, large hydro accounted for 51.96 GW, and small hydro accounted for 5.18 GW. The expansion of renewable energy installations is relevant for cable demand across project sites, pooling substations, evacuation lines, storage integration, and grid interconnection infrastructure. 4. Distribution Network Modernisation and Smart Metering Power distribution reforms are creating demand for distribution infrastructure, feeder-level systems, smart metering infrastructure, and associated cabling. Under the distribution reform programme, infrastructure works including smart metering works worth Rs 2.8 lakh crore have been sanctioned. This includes Rs 1.53 lakh crore for loss-reduction infrastructure and Rs 1.31 lakh crore for smart metering. Smart metering works have been sanctioned for 19.79 crore consumers, 2.11 lakh feeders, and 52.53 lakh distribution transformers, totalling 20.33 crore smart meters. These works include replacement of old conductors, augmentation of substations and distribution transformers, creation of new substations, feeder segregation, and implementation of monitoring systems, all of which are relevant to wires, cables, conductors, and allied electrical products. 5. Railway Electrification and Transport Infrastructure Railway electrification remains an important demand driver for traction cables, signalling cables, control cables, overhead equipment, and power-supply infrastructure. As of 31 December 2025, 69,712 route kilometres of the broad-gauge railway network had been electrified, representing 99.4% electrification. Railway electrification during 2014–25 stood at 46,900 route kilometres, compared with 21,801 route kilometres before 2014. The continued electrification of balance sections and construction of new electrified lines supports ongoing demand for power and control cabling across railway infrastructure. 6. Digital Connectivity and Optical Fibre Expansion Digital infrastructure expansion is supporting demand for optical fibre cables and related network cabling. Under BharatNet, 2,14,325 Gram Panchayats had been connected, and 6,93,303 km of optical fibre cable had been laid as of 26 May 2025. The amended broadband programme is also being implemented to strengthen rural broadband connectivity, with the objective of optical fibre connectivity to approximately 2.64 lakh Gram Panchayats and demand-based connectivity to around 3.8 lakh villages. This creates a continued requirement for optical fibre cable, network accessories, last-mile connectivity components, and maintenance-related cabling infrastructure. 7. Risks and Challenges to the Product of the Issuer Company • Dependence on Government and Utility Projects: The company derives a significant portion of its business from power infrastructure, electrification, substation, and distribution projects that are typically awarded by government departments and state utilities. Any reduction in government spending, delays in tender issuance, policy changes, or cancellation of schemes may adversely impact order inflows and revenue visibility. Additionally, payment delays from government entities could strain the company's cash flows and working capital position. • Project Execution and Completion Risk: The company operates in the EPC segment, where successful execution depends on timely availability of materials, labour, site access, and regulatory approvals. Delays arising from land acquisition issues, contractor disputes, logistics disruptions, or adverse weather conditions may lead to cost overruns and contractual penalties. Failure to execute projects within stipulated timelines could negatively affect profitability and reputation. • Raw Material Price Volatility: Manufacturing of cables, conductors, and other electrical products requires key raw materials such as copper, aluminium, and PVC compounds. Significant fluctuations in commodity prices can increase input costs and compress margins, particularly under fixed-price contracts where cost escalation may not 216 be recoverable. Sustained inflation in raw material prices could adversely affect the company's financial performance. • High Working Capital Requirements: The EPC and infrastructure business is inherently working-capital intensive, requiring substantial upfront expenditure on procurement, inventory, and project execution before receiving customer payments. Delays in certification of work or collection of receivables can lead to liquidity pressures. The company may therefore require continuous access to debt and banking facilities to support business growth and operations. • Intense Competitive Environment: The company faces competition from established cable manufacturers, EPC contractors, and integrated infrastructure companies with larger scale, stronger financial resources, and longer operating track records. Competitive bidding for government and utility contracts can put pressure on margins and reduce the likelihood of securing new projects. Inability to compete effectively may impact market share and future growth prospects. •Regulatory and Sector-Specific Risks: The power infrastructure sector is highly regulated and subject to changes in government policies, electrical safety standards, environmental norms, and procurement regulations. Any adverse regulatory changes could increase compliance costs or delay project approvals. Moreover, evolving technologies in renewable energy, smart grids, and power distribution may require additional investments to remain competitive. 8. Peak energy demand grew at a CAGR of 5.2% from FY21 to FY26 and is expected to grow at a CAGR of 7.9% by FY32 reaching 388 GW. Rising peak electricity demand is expected to structurally support solar capacity addition in India, as solar is one of the fastest deployable and cost-competitive sources for meeting incremental daytime demand from commercial, industrial, agricultural and cooling loads. India’s power requirement recorded a steady CAGR of 6.0% during FY21-FY26. Over the same period, the gap between electricity requirement and supply narrowed sharply, declining from 5 BU in FY21 to nearly 0 BU in FY26, reflecting a significant improvement in supply adequacy and system reliability. Rapid capacity addition, especially in renewable energy and steady growth in thermal power improved overall power availability. Manufacturing Process We manufacture a range of electrical products, including PVC insulated (HD) electric cables, XLPE insulated PVC sheathed cables, LT XLPE aerial bunched cables, PVC insulated U/A cables and ACSR and AAAC conductors. Our manufacturing capabilities are supported by in-house processes for conductor formation, insulation, cable construction, testing and finishing, enabling us to manufacture products in accordance with applicable technical specifications and customer requirements. The manufacturing process is designed around a systematic sequence of raw material inspection, wire drawing, conductor formation, insulation and cable construction, followed by testing, marking, packing and dispatch. The precise manufacturing route varies depending upon the type, construction, voltage rating, application and technical specifications of the product. For conductors, the process generally involves wire drawing, testing and stranding to achieve the required conductor size and construction. Depending on the cable construction, further processes may include laying-up of cores, screening, inner sheathing, armouring and application of the outer sheath. The sequence and processes vary depending on the type of product being manufactured. The manufacturing process is supported by in-process inspection and testing at relevant stages, followed by finished-product testing to assess conformity with the applicable product specifications and standards. After completion of testing, the finished products are packed in the required form and dispatched to customers. Our specified products are manufactured under applicable BIS licences and standards, and the Company has undertaken type testing of its cable products through recognised testing facilities, as applicable to the respective products. 239 Raw Material Procurement The manufacturing process commences with the procurement of key raw materials required for manufacturing Cables and Conductors. Depending upon the product being manufactured, these may include aluminium and copper rods, PVC and XLPE compounds, galvanized steel wires or strips and other specified materials. This stage also involves appropriate inspection and quality checks Wire Drawing Aluminium or copper rods are processed through the wire drawing process, wherein the cross-sectional diameter of the rod is progressively reduced through suitable drawing dies to achieve the required wire diameter. The process enables the production of conductor wires of specified dimensions and characteristics. Appropriate process controls are undertaken during wire drawing to maintain dimensional consistency and ensure that the processed wire meets the prescribed requirements. Conductor Manufacturing Following wire drawing, individual conductor wires are assembled and twisted in a predetermined configuration through the stranding or bunching process to determine the formation of a conductor having the required cross-sectional area, flexibility and electrical characteristics. The number, arrangement and construction of wires are 240 determined by the required conductor size, design and applicable technical specifications. Insulation and Sheathing The conductor is passed through an extrusion process in which the specified insulating compound, such as XLPE or PVC, is applied uniformly around the conductor to provide the required electrical separation and protection and is applied in accordance with the applicable voltage rating, cable construction and technical specifications. Where applicable, an inner sheath or bedding layer is provided over the laid-up cores, which provides for the separation and protection between the insulated cores and subsequent layers of the cable and prepares the cable for armouring or outer sheathing. Such outer sheath forms the external protective layer of the cable and contributes to its durability during transportation, installation and operation. Testing The completed conductors undergo applicable quality checks and testing, including relevant dimensional, electrical and mechanical tests, as prescribed for the particular product. Products conforming to the applicable specifications are cleared for further processing or, where the conductor constitutes the final product, for coiling or drumming and dispatch. Depending upon the product and applicable standards, testing may also include relevant electrical, dimensional, physical and mechanical tests, as well as other prescribed routine or acceptance tests. Process-level quality checks enable identification of deviations during manufacturing and facilitate corrective action before the product proceeds to the next stage of production. Finishing The finished Cables and Conductors are subjected to applicable final inspection and testing prior to release for packing and dispatch. The specific tests undertaken vary according to the product category, applicable standards and customer requirements. Furthermore, the finished products are appropriately marked and labelled with relevant product identification and other prescribed information. Packing and Dispatch Depending upon the product configuration, finished Cables and Conductors are packed in coils, drums or other suitable packaging to facilitate safe storage, handling and transportation. The finished products are thereafter dispatched to customers in accordance with the applicable purchase orders, technical specifications and delivery schedules.
