Opportunity and Bidding a. Identification of Opportunities and Projects Governmental and PSU tenders are a primary source for identifying commercial opportunities for EPC and project development companies wherein the Business Development team continuously monitors opportunities from: (i) NTPC / NTPC Renewable Energy, (ii) Coal India and its subsidiaries, (iii) SECI, (iv) State DISCOMs, (v) State Renewable Energy Agencies, (vi) State Power Generation Companies, (vii) State Transmission Utilities, (viii) CPSUs and other government organizations and (ix) Central Public Procurement Portal and state e-procurement portals. For business opportunities at the state level, there exist similar schemes and projects such as: (i) State DISCOM procurement plans, (ii) PM-KUSUM Scheme, (iii) Feeder solarisation, (iv) RESCO/CAPEX opportunities and (v) Open-access and C&I opportunities. b. Initial Opportunity Screening Each identified opportunity is subject to preliminary screening before significant management time and resources are committed. The screening considers the project capacity, including MW, MWp or MWh; project location; the client,; contract type; tariff or EPC price and resulting commercial attractiveness; land availability and whether it is client-provided, private or government land; grid connectivity, including voltage level and substation availability; technical and financial qualification requirements; expected bidders and market competition; financing through equity, debt, VGF or subsidy; and key risks relating to land, grid, PPA, approvals, tariff and timelines. c. Technical/Commercial Due Diligence Once a project successfully clears the initial screening, the same undergoes a due diligence process to determine whether the project can actually be developed and commissioned within the proposed cost and timeline. Technical due diligence covers site assessment, including site location and accessibility, land area and ownership, topography, soil conditions, flooding and drainage, approach roads, nearby infrastructure, water availability, and shadow and obstruction analysis. We also mainly conduct Grid Connectivity and Land Diligence for Solar EPC projects wherein the relevant teams verify evacuation capacity, transmission voltage, connectivity approval and metering requirements for Grid Connectivity diligence and also conducts verification of ownership/titles, land records, lease agreements, land-use conversions, agricultural/non-agricultural status and right of way among 252 others. d. Tender/Project Evaluation Once the tender is published, Business Development works jointly with the technical, procurement, finance and management teams to conduct tender studies, QR assessment, BOQ analysis, technical compliance, vendor enquiries, risk loading, financial modelling, management approval and price strategy. The final bid price is not based only on market competition and takes into consideration the actual project cost, supplier quotations, commodity prices, module pricing, financing cost, working capital, construction timeline, liquidated damages, warranty obligations, O&M liability, escalation risk and currency risk. e. Bid/Proposal Preparation Once the tender has been evaluated to ensure viability, the preparation of the bid begins with a detailed review of the eligibility criteria, scope of work, technical specifications, contractual conditions, timelines and payment terms. Following this, detailed assessment of technical and financial qualification requirements, compilation with mandatory documents and annexures, preparation of BOQ, technical proposals and compliance statements along detailed project costing is undertaken by the Company. Following this entire process, the bid is drafted and prepared for submission through the relevant tender portal post the final technical and commercial review. f. Management Review and Approval The management of the Company undertakes a comprehensive assessment of the project’s strategic fit, eligibility-building potential and its potential to establish or strengthen relationships with its clients. This review is made not only from the perspective of immediate project profitability but also from the perspective of its long-term strategic benefits to the Company, considering commercial viability, project cost, expected margins, payment terms and working capital requirements, along with the potential contribution of the project towards maintaining or increasing annual turnover, revenue and profitability. Additionally, the Company’s management also considers future business potential, repeat orders, future tenders, O&M opportunities and long-term business relationships, together with contractual, technical, financing, execution and other project risks. g. Bid Submission/Commercial Negotiation The activities undertaken during the pre-bid stage culminate in the submission of the bid based on the assessment of the project’s technical and commercial feasibility, applicable qualification requirements, project costs, associated risks and the proposed pricing strategy. Meanwhile, negotiation covers price, quantity discounts, payment terms, delivery commitments, warranty, spare parts, testing, site support, freight, escalation protection and delay provisions. For large EPC projects, payment terms can materially affect working capital. Depending on contractual arrangements, payment mechanisms may include advance payment, payment against dispatch documents, credit period and bank-guarantees. Post-Bid h. Project Planning and Mobilisation The procurement process starts after project award or receipt of a firm requirement from the project and engineering teams. The requirements comprise approved drawings, technical specifications, BOQ, MTO, datasheets, approved makes/vendor lists, project schedule and delivery priorities. Project planning thus converts project requirements into a structured purchasing strategy aligned with the master project schedule decided upon during the bidding process. i. Engineering and Procurement Procurement involves identification of manufacturers, OEMs, distributors, suppliers and subcontractors, as the evaluated based on technical capability and their ability to meet specifications and standards; manufacturing capacity and ability to meet project quantity and schedule; financial strength and ability to execute large orders; quality systems, including QA/QC systems, certifications and traceability; experience and similar project references; delivery performance, including historical lead-time and service support, including technical support and after-sales service; warranty. 253 j. Project Execution Project execution involves various steps in its ambit, such as quality control, safety and client coordination. Quality is controlled at the stages of document review, raw material, in-process inspection, final inspection, factory acceptance testing and site receipt. Safety protocols are also designed, not just for the workers and employees but also to protect the Company. k. Testing and Commissioning Testing and Commissioning involves the verification that the completed project has been installed, tested and commissioned in accordance with the contractual requirements, approved designs, technical specifications and applicable standards set across in the bid by the clients. The process includes inspection and testing of major equipment and electrical, mechanical and safety systems, verification of commissioning timelines and power generation performance by the clients along with the closure of punch points and submission of relevant test reports, as-built drawings, warranties and O&M documentation within the prescribed contractual commissioning timeline. Upon satisfactory completion, the client issues the Commissioning/Acceptance Certificate, formally recognizing the project as commissioned in accordance with the contractual obligations. l. Billing and Collection Upon arrival, materials are verified for quantity, condition, documentation and specification before acceptance. The process includes document checking, quantity verification, visual/damage inspection, technical/document verification, GRN preparation and issuance of an NCR/claim for rejected or damaged material. Payment is linked to the purchase order, receipt/acceptance and contractual milestones. The process comprises the purchase order, GRN and tax invoice, followed by three-way matching, payment approval and the payment/financing process. m. Handover and Project Closure The final stage in the project cycle, handover involves the closure of client observations and punch points, along with the completion of the project and associated facilities, submission of testing, commissioning and as-built documentation and confirmation of applicable statutory and regulatory compliances. The Company also undertakes O&M mobilization and conducts a joint inspection with the client to ensure that there are no discrepancies before the handover. Upon the satisfactory completion of all contractual obligations and documentation, the Handover/Take-Over Certificate or Completion Certificate is obtained from the client, marking formal project closure and commencement of the O&M period, as applicable. INDUSTRY SPECIFIC LAWS The Electricity Act, 2003 ("Electricity Act") The Electricity Act is a central legislation and provides for, among others, generation, transmission, distribution, trading and use of electricity and generally for taking measures conducive to development of electricity industry. Under the Electricity Act, the transmission, distribution, and trade of electricity are regulated activities which require licenses from the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission ("CERC"), the State Electricity Regulatory Commissions ("SERCs") or a joint commission (constituted by an agreement entered into between two or more State Governments or the Central Government in relation to one or more State Governments, as the case may be). The Electricity Act consolidates the laws relating to generation, transmission, distribution, trading and use of electricity. It lays down provisions in relation to transmission and distribution of electricity. It states that the State Government can specify suitable measures for specifying action to be taken in relation to any electric line or electrical plant, or any electrical appliance under the control of a consumer for the purpose of eliminating or reducing the risk of personal injury or damage to property or interference with its use. Further, the act covers that electrical contractors must comply with licensing requirements stipulated by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) and respective State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) to work on high-voltage systems and major electrical infrastructure projects. The act mandates adherence to safety standards, precautions, and practices during the installation, operation, and maintenance of electrical systems to avoid accidents, electrical fires, and damage to equipment. Any electrical installation above a certain voltage level (e.g., 415V or 650V) must be certified by a licensed electrical contractor. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (“MNRE”) The MNRE is the nodal ministry of the Government of India at the national level for all matters relating to nonconventional sources of energy and renewable energy. The mandate of MNRE includes research, development, commercialisation and deployment of renewable energy systems or devices for various applications in rural, urban, industrial and commercial sector National Electricity Policy The GoI notified the National Electricity Policy on February 12, 2005, in accordance with the provisions of the Electricity Act. The National Electricity Policy provides guidelines for accelerated development of the power sector, providing supply of electricity to all areas and protecting interests of consumers and other stakeholders keeping in view availability of energy resources, technology available to exploit these resources, economics of generation using different resources, and energy security issues. The National Electricity Policy provides that the SERCs should specify appropriate tariffs in order to promote renewable energy, up until renewable energy power producers relying on non-conventional technologies can compete with conventional sources of energy. The 259 SERCs are required to ensure progressive increase in the share of generation of electricity from non-conventional sources and provide suitable measures for connectivity with grid and sale of electricity to any person. Further, the SERCs are required to specify, for the purchase of electricity from renewable energy sources, a percentage of the total consumption of electricity in a distribution licensee. Furthermore, the National Electricity Policy provides that such purchase of electricity by distribution companies should be through a competitive bidding process. The National Electricity Policy permits the SERCs to determine appropriate differential prices for the purchase of electricity from renewable energy power producers, in order to promote renewable sources of energy. Electricity (Promoting Renewable Energy Through Green Energy Open Access) Rules, 2022 The Ministry of Power, Government of India ("MoP"), has notified the Electricity (Promoting Renewable Energy Through Green Energy Open Access) Rules, 2022 in exercise of the powers conferred under the Electricity Act, 2003. The Green Energy Open Access Rules provide a comprehensive framework governing the generation, purchase, and consumption of green energy, including energy derived from waste-to-energy plants. The Rules lay down detailed provisions covering renewable purchase obligations (RPO), green energy open access, the role of nodal agencies, the process for obtaining green energy open access, the issuance of green certificates, energy banking arrangements, applicable open access charges, and cross-subsidy surcharges. Additionally, the Rules provides for tariff for green energy, which is to be fixed by the relevant regulatory commission. It will be calculated based on the average pooled power purchase cost of the renewable energy, cross-subsidy charges, and service charges that account for the reasonable costs incurred by the distribution licensee in supplying green energy to consumers. Approved Models and Manufacturers of Solar Photovoltaic Modules (Requirement for Compulsory Registration) Order, 2019 (“ALMM Order”) To ensure the quality of solar cells and solar modules, used in solar PV power plants, the MNRE issued the “Approved List of models and manufacturers” (“ALMM”) Order on January 2, 2019. The ALMM Order provides that only the models and manufacturers included in the ALMM, which is a list of eligible models and manufacturers complying with BIS standards, would be eligible for use in government/government assisted projects under government schemes and programmes installed in the country, including projects set-up for sale of electricity to the government under the “Guidelines for Tariff Based Competitive Bidding Process for Procurement of Power from Grid Connected Solar PV Power Projects” dated August 3, 2017 and the amendments thereof (collectively, the “Applicable Projects”). The ALMM consists of List I, specifying models and manufacturers of solar PV modules and List II specifying models and manufacturers of solar PV cells. After March 31, 2020, solar PV module manufacturers in List I have to mandatorily source PV solar cells only from manufacturers in List II for the Applicable Projects. Manufacturers are required to make an application to the MNRE for inclusion in the ALMM. For being eligible to be included in List-I, the manufacturers are required to obtain a BIS certification in accordance with the Compulsory Registration Order. Before inclusion in the ALMM, a MNRE team will conduct inspection of the manufacturingfacilityofmanufacturerswhosemodelsarecertified/registeredundertheCompulsory Registration Order. If enlisted, such enlistment shall be valid for a two-year period and can be renewed by submitting necessary documents and continued satisfactory performance of their products. Enlisted models and manufacturers will be subjected to random quality tests, and any failure or non-compliance will lead to removal from the ALMM. The Central Electricity Authority (Measures Relating to Safety and Electric Supply) Regulations, 2023 ("CEA Regulations") The Central Electricity Authority (Measures relating to Safety and Electric Supply) Regulations, 2023 apply to electrical installations and prescribe safety and standards-conformance requirements for materials, apparatus and installation and maintenance, including requirements for ratings, insulation, mechanical strength and certain switchgear and fireproof enclosure requirements at consumer premises. The CEA Regulations supersede the Central Electricity Authority (Measures relating to Safety and Electric Supply) Regulations, 2010. The CEA Regulations are applicable to electrical installation including electrical plant and electric line, and the person engaged in the generation, transmission, distribution, trading, supply or use of electricity. They mandate periodic inspection, accident reporting, safety audits and the use of qualified technical personnel, and empower the CEA and designated authorities to enforce compliance and provide for penalties in case of contravention. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Indian Electricity Grid Code) Regulations, 2023 260 The CERC issued the CERC (Indian Electricity Grid Code) Regulations, 2023 which came into effect on October 1, 2023. These regulations aim to promote a stable, reliable, and secure grid while achieving maximum economy and efficiency in grid operations and the power system. The Central Electricity Authority (Technical Standards for Construction of Electrical Plants and Electric Lines) Regulations, 2022 The Central Electricity Authority (Technical Standards for Construction of Electrical Plants and Electric Lines) Regulations,2022, set out the technical standards and specifications for the design, construction, and testing of electrical plants and electric lines across India. These regulations aim to ensure safety, reliability, and efficiency in the power system infrastructure. They cover aspects such as conductor specifications, clearance requirements, earthing, protection systems, and environmental considerations, providing a uniform framework to be followed by generating companies, transmission licensees, and distribution utilities. The Central Electricity Authority (Technical Standards for Connectivity to the Grid) Regulations, 2007 The Central Electricity Authority (Technical Standards for Connectivity to the Grid) Regulations, 2007, issued under the Electricity Act, 2003, establish technical, operational, and safety requirements for connecting generating stations, transmission lines, distribution systems, bulk consumers, and energy storage systems to the electricity grid. These regulations set standards for equipment design, protection systems, communication, cyber security, power quality, and operational coordination, ensuring grid reliability, stability, and safety. Compliance includes signing connection agreements, providing real-time data, following specified protection and metering norms, meeting voltage, frequency, and harmonics limits, and adhering to special provisions for renewable energy, transmission substations, and distribution networks. Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020 The Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020, notified by the MoP on December 31, 2020, provide a framework for consumer participation in electricity generation through net metering, gross metering, and net billing. Under net metering, consumers (prosumers) with sanctioned loads up to 500 kW can offset their electricity consumption with energy generated from rooftop solar, with surplus carried forward for future billing cycles. Gross metering requires all generated power to be fed into the grid, and the consumer is compensated at a regulated feed-in tariff while continuing to purchase electricity separately. Net billing, or net feed-in, allows self-consumption of solar energy, with any surplus exported to the grid being monetarily credited at a tariff set by the SERC, instead of a unit-to-unit adjustment. These mechanisms are subject to state-specific regulations and are aimed at promoting RE while protecting consumer rights. Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan Scheme 2019 (“PM-KUSUM”) The PM-KUSUM scheme was implemented by the MNRE in 2019 with three components: (i) Component A -For setting up of 10,000 MW of decentralised grid connected renewable energy power plants on barren land. Under this component, renewable energy-based power plants (REPP) of capacity 500 KW to 2 MW will be set up by individual farmers / group of farmers / cooperatives / panchayats / farmer producer organisations (FPO) / water user associations (WUA) on barren land. Under this component, individual farmers having grid connected agriculture pumps will be supported to solarise pumps. The farmers will be able to use the generated solar power to meet their irrigation needs and excess power will be sold to DISCOMs at pre-fixed tariff. Solar Park Scheme The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (“MNRE”) has drawn a scheme to set up number of solar parks across various states in the country, each with a capacity of Solar Projects generally above 500 MW. The Scheme proposes to provide financial support by Government of India to establish solar parks with an aim to facilitate creation of infrastructure necessary for setting up new solar power projects in terms of allocation of land, transmission and evacuation lines, access roads, availability of water and others, in a focused manner. At the state level, the solar park will enable the states to bring in significant investment from project developers in the Solar Power sector, to meet its Solar Purchase Obligation (“SPO”) mandates and provide employment opportunities to local population. The state will also be able to reduce its carbon footprint by avoiding emissions equivalent to the solar park’s generated capacity. Renewable Purchase Obligations The Electricity Act and the National Tariff Policy require the SERCs to specify, for the purchase of electricity from renewable energy sources, a minimum percentage of the total consumption of electricity within the area of a distribution licensee, which are known as renewable purchase obligations (“RPOs”). RPOs are required to be met by obligated entities (distribution licensees, captive power plants and open access consumers) by purchasing renewable energy, either by renewable energy power producers such as the Company and its Subsidiaries, or by purchasing renewable energy certificates. In the event of default by an obligated entity in any fiscal year, the SERCs may direct the obligated entity to pay a penalty or to deposit an amount determined by the relevant SERC, into a fund to be utilized for, among others, the purchase of renewable energy certificates. Labour Codes In order to rationalise and reform labour laws in India, the Government of India has framed four labour codes which (barring certain provisions) have been brought into effect, through a notification, from November 21, 2025, namely: 1. The Code on Wages, 2019 The Code on Wages, 2019 consolidates laws relating to wages, subsuming the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. The Code provides for a new definition of 'wages' and minimum wages to be notified for all employees in all industries, based on the categories of employees and/or geographical locations and other conditions of service, which shall be equal to or above the rate of floor wages set by the Central Government, and further mandates fixation of wage period and timely wage payment. It also requires that pay parity should be ensured for all genders, provides for payment of annual bonus, and normal working hours to be prescribed, with the requirement to pay overtime at twice the normal pay rates in the event an employee works beyond the normal working hours. 2. The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 consolidates and amends laws relating to trade unions, conditions of employment in industrial establishments and undertakings, and industrial disputes, subsuming the Trade Unions Act, 1926, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The key provisions include (i) recognition of negotiating union and negotiating council; (ii) specific recognition of fixed-term employment with equal benefits including parity in wages, working hours and allowances with permanent workers; (iii) definitions of key terms including 'employee' and 'worker'; (iv) conditions for lay-offs, retrenchment and closure, including increase in the headcount threshold from 100 to 300 workers for applicability of certain special provisions to factories, mines and plantations; (v) constitution of a grievance redressal committee with equal employer and employee representation; (vi) mandatory notice requirements for strikes and lock-outs in all industrial establishments; (vii) provision of notice to workers prior to change in certain conditions of service; (viii) prohibition of identified unfair labour practices; (ix) adoption and certification of standing orders; and (x) dispute resolution through conciliation, labour courts and industrial tribunals. 3. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 consolidates occupational safety, health and working conditions laws, consolidating several central labour laws including the Factories Act, 1948, the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, the Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979, and the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996, amongst others. The Occupational Safety Code provides for definitions of key terms including 'contract labour', 'contractor', 'principal employer' and 'establishment'; annual leave with wages; prescription of working hours and rest intervals; special provisions on employment of women in night shifts; and prescription of health and safety obligations and provision of welfare facilities. It also provides for a common registration to be obtained by establishments (including factories and commercial establishments), a licence for contractors supplying contract labour, and scope for prescription of requirement for factories to obtain specific licences. 4. The Code on Social Security, 2020 264 The Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes several social security-related legislations including the Employee's Compensation Act, 1923, the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948, the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, the Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act, 1959, the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 and the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. The Code on Social Security, 2020 consolidates social security laws and governs social security organisations and benefits, including provident fund, pension, employees' deposit-linked insurance, employees' state insurance coverage and benefits including sickness benefit and disablement benefit, compensation to be paid to employees for workplace injuries and occupational diseases, maternity benefits, gratuity payments including to fixed-term employees, and prescription of social security benefits for unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers. The above-mentioned labour codes are not intended to subsume state-specific laws. Further, notwithstanding the introduction of the new labour codes, anything done or any action taken under the enactments repealed shall be in force to the extent they are not contrary to the provisions of the above-mentioned labour codes. ENVIRONMENTAL LAWS The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 ("EP Act"), Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986 ("EP Rules") and the Environmental Impact Assessment Notification, 2006 ("EIA Notification") The EPA is designed to safeguard and enhance environmental quality, combat pollution, and authorize governmental intervention for environmental protection. The Act mandates that no entity involved in industry, operations, or processes shall release or allow the release of any environmental pollutant exceeding prescribed standards. Furthermore, it prohibits the handling of hazardous substances except in compliance with specified procedures and safeguards. The EPA grants authority to the Central Government to implement measures necessary for environmental protection, including setting emission standards, imposing restrictions on industrial locations, and overall pollution control. Violation of the provisions of EPA and the rules thereunder can result in the imposition of penalty which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees and can also extend to fifteen lakh rupees, and in case the failure or contravention continues, with additional fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees for every day during which such failure or contravention continues after the conviction for the first such failure or contravention. Additionally, under the EIA Notification and its subsequent amendments, projects are required to mandatorily obtain environmental clearance from the concerned authorities depending on the potential impact on human health and resources. Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 ("Water Act") 265 The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 establishes state pollution control boards to regulate discharges and requires consent and compliance with standards, with a tiered penalty structure including fines and imprisonment and additional daily fines for continuing offences. The Water Act prohibits the use of any stream or well for the disposal of polluting matter in violation of the standards set by the State Pollution Control Board ("State PCB"). The Water Act also provides that the consent of the State PCB must be obtained prior to establishing any industry, operation or process which is likely to discharge sewage effluent. Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 ("Air Act") The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 empowers state pollution control boards to inspect, issue directions and require consents in air pollution control areas, with emissions standards and penalties including for continuing offences. Any person establishing or operating any industrial plant within an air pollution control area must obtain the consent of the relevant State PCB prior to establishing or operating such industrial plant. No person operating any industrial plant in any air pollution control area shall discharge or permit the emission of any air pollutant in excess of the standards laid down by the State PCB. Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 ("Noise Regulation Rules") The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 (as amended) regulate noise levels, specify ambient standards and silence zones, and provide for penalties including fines up to ₹1 lakh and additional daily fines for continuing violations. The Noise Regulation Rules regulate and control noise-producing and generating sources including from industrial activity, and set ambient air quality standards in respect of noise for different areas and zones. Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 ("Public Liability Act") The Public Liability Act imposes liability on the owner or controller of hazardous substances for any damage arising out of an accident involving such hazardous substance. The owner or handler is also required to take out an insurance policy insuring against liability under the legislation. The rules made under the Public Liability Act mandate that the employer has to contribute a sum equal to the premium paid on the insurance policies towards the environment relief fund. The Competition Act establishes the CCI to prevent practices adverse to competition, addresses anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominance and regulation of combinations, provides for show-cause and investigation processes for combinations where an appreciable adverse effect on competition ("AAEC") is suspected, and prescribes fines for non-compliance with CCI directions including daily fines up to a maximum amount. The Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 introduces key changes including a deal value threshold of ₹2,000 crores for reporting mergers and acquisitions, reduces the merger review timeline from 210 to 150 days, broadens the scope of anti-competitive agreements (including "exclusive dealing"), expands the cartel definition to include hub-and-spoke arrangements, and provides the CCI the power to impose penalties based on a company's global turnover for anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominant position. INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY AND DATA PROTECTION LAWS The Information Technology Act, 2000 ("IT Act") The IT Act is the primary legislation regulating electronic records and addresses, among other things, electronic signatures, unauthorised access, processing of sensitive personal data, and intermediary obligations. The IT Act provides a safe harbour for intermediaries where the intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system and the intermediary does not initiate transmissions, select the recipient, or select or modify information in transmissions. Entities must also comply with CERT-In Directions under the IT Act governing cybersecurity, breach reporting, record maintenance and point of contact requirements, and the July 25, 2025 "Comprehensive Cyber Security Audit Policy Guidelines" requiring, amongst other things, a management-approved audit programme, implementation of recommendations and follow-ups. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 ("DPDP Act") and Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 ("DPDP Rules") The Government notified the DPDP Act (2023) and the DPDP Rules (November 13, 2025), with an 18-month implementation timeline from November 2025; provisions establishing administrative machinery such as the Data Protection Board of India are in force from November 13, 2025, consent manager provisions come into force within one year (November 2026), and entities have until May 2027 to comply with substantive obligations. The DPDP Framework imposes obligations on "data fiduciaries" (entities determining the means and purposes of processing personal data), including consent and notice requirements, ensuring completeness, accuracy and consistency of data, breach notifications, and technical safeguards and reasonable security measures. It also provides additional obligations for "significant data fiduciaries" (to be notified by the Government) such as appointing a Data Protection Officer, an independent data auditor, conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments and periodic audits, based on factors including the volume and sensitivity of data processed, risk to data principals and potential impact on sovereignty and integrity, electoral democracy, State security and public order. CONSUMER PROTECTION LAWS The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 Entities involved in marketing, sale or distribution of goods and services must comply with the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and rules thereunder, and must refrain from restrictive or unfair trade practices, unfair contracts, deficient services, overcharging beyond legal or agreed pricing, offering hazardous services with knowledge, misleading advertisements prejudicial to consumers, and violations of consumer rights. Service providers must also comply with advertising regulations including the Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements for Misleading Advertisements, 2022 and the ASCI Code for Self-Regulation, and must additionally comply with the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 prohibiting user interface and user experience practices designed to mislead or trick users into unintended actions. 267 LAWS APPLICABLE TO US FOR LISTING OF OUR EQUITY SHARES ON THE STOCK EXCHANGES SEBI Act and Regulations From time to time, our Company will be required to comply with various regulations notified by the SEBI including the SEBI Act, the SCRA, the SEBI Listing Regulations, SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, the SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices) Regulations, 2003, the SEBI ICDR Regulations and SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefits and Sweat Equity) Regulations, 2021, to the extent applicable. Set out below is a summary of these regulations: Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 (“SEBI Act”) The SEBI Act establishes SEBI as the principal regulatory authority overseeing India’s securities markets. It confers comprehensive powers upon SEBI to regulate all facets of securities markets, including issuance, listing, and trading activities. The SEBI Act authorizes SEBI to safeguard investor interests, maintain market integrity, and foster market development through regulations, circulars, and guidelines. Furthermore, it empowers SEBI to conduct investigations into potential violations, impose administrative and monetary sanctions, and pursue enforcement actions against non-compliant market participants. Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 (“SCRA”) The SCRA regulates securities transactions and establishes the legal infrastructure for stock exchanges within India. It comprehensively defines securities and financial instruments while governing listing requirements and prohibiting unauthorized trading. The SCRA establishes parameters for recognition of Stock Exchanges and empowers the Central Government and SEBI to implement measures for intervention when necessary to protect investor interests or preserve market stability. It also provides the statutory basis for regulation of derivatives and other complex financial instruments. Securities and Exchange Board of India (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 (“SEBI ICDR Regulations”) The SEBI ICDR Regulations regulate the issuance of equity and convertible securities and prescribe disclosure requirements for companies raising funds through various channels including, inter alia, an initial public offer, further public offer, rights issue and qualified institutional placement. It sets out the guidelines and framework that companies must follow to issue equity and convertible securities to the public. It also prescribes disclosure requirements relating to material information, risks, and details regarding the financial condition of the company in connection with such issuances. Securities and Exchange Board of India (Share Based Employee Benefits and Sweat Equity) Regulations, 2021 (“SEBI SBEB & SE Regulations”) The SEBI SBEB & SE Regulations govern share-based employee benefit schemes of equity listed companies. It is applicable to an equity listed company that seeks to issue sweat equity shares or has a scheme: (i) for direct or indirect benefit of employees; (ii) involving dealing in, subscribing to or purchasing securities of the company, directly or indirectly; and (iii) satisfying, directly or indirectly, any one of the following conditions: the scheme is set up by the company or any other company in its group; the scheme is funded or guaranteed by the company or any other company in its group; or the scheme is controlled or managed by the company or any other company in its group. SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI LODR Regulations”) The SEBI LODR Regulations ensure that all listed companies adhere to uniform standards of transparency, disclosure, and corporate governance, thereby protecting investor interests and maintaining market integrity. The regulations govern financial disclosures, board composition, shareholder rights, related party transactions, and timely reporting of material events. Non-compliance with SEBI LODR Regulations can attract monetary penalties, suspension of trading, freezing of promoter shareholding, or even delisting of securities, making strict adherence essential for any listed entity. 268 Securities and Exchange Board of India (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI PIT Regulations”) The SEBI PIT Regulations aim to curb trading based on unpublished price-sensitive information (“UPSI”). The regulations define who qualifies as an ‘insider’ and prohibit such persons from dealing in securities while in possession of UPSI. Listed companies must implement a code of conduct, maintain a digital database of information sharing, and define trading windows for employees. The framework ensures fair trading and confidence in market integrity. Violation of SEBI PIT Regulations can result in penalties and/or criminal action. Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 (“SEBI SAST Regulations”) The SEBI SAST Regulations govern the acquisition of shares or control in listed companies. Acquirers who cross specific thresholds must make an open offer to public shareholders to give them an exit option. The regulations ensure that all takeovers or control changes are transparent and equitable. The regulations include detailed timelines, pricing norms, and disclosure requirements. These regulations are critical in maintaining fairness during mergers, acquisitions, and hostile takeovers. Securities and Exchange Board of India (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003 (“SEBI FUTP Regulations”) The SEBI FUTP Regulations prevent manipulative and unethical practices such as price rigging, pump and dump schemes, circular trading, front-running, and misrepresentation, among others. These regulations empower SEBI to investigate and act against any unfair conduct. The law is designed to maintain orderly market conditions and protect the interests of retail investors. Violations under SEBI FUTP Regulations can lead to penalties, bans, and criminal prosecution. These rules are essential to sustaining investor trust, deterring manipulative behaviours and maintaining market efficiency. OVERVIEW We are an engineering, procurement and construction (“EPC”) company with operations across solar energy projects, electricity distribution & transmission, and water infrastructure solutions. We undertake central government funded EPC projects for state government entities, government undertakings, power utilities and other institutional customers. Our clients include public sector entities such as New & Renewable Energy Department, Haryana/HAREDA, Madhya Pradesh Urja Vikas Nigam Limited, Tripura Renewable Energy Development Agency, Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited, Maharashtra State Power Generation Company Limited, Rajasthan Renewable Energy Corporation Limited, Kerala State Electricity Board Limited and Jodhpur Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited. We are also in the business of manufacturing electrical Cables and Conductors since 2006, which are deployed in the power utility and infrastructure sectors. Our product portfolio includes PVC insulated (HD) electric cables, XLPE insulated PVC sheathed cables, LT XLPE aerial bunched cables, PVC insulated U/A cables and ACSR and AAAC conductors which are manufactured in our facility at Sitapura Industrial Area, Jaipur, Rajasthan. Our revenue from operations and EBITDA grew at a CAGR of 22.09% and 41.46% respectively in last three years. We achieved an 356 average PAT Margin of 7.61% in the last three year, along with an average RoE and RoCE at 50.79% and 44.52% respectively between FY24 to FY26. (Source: CARE Report) We operate across two key business segments: (i) EPC Services and (ii) Manufacturing: EPC Project Services Our EPC projects vertical comprises of Solar, Electrical and Water projects. We provide end-to-end services, depending on the scope of the relevant contract, from design and engineering, procurement and supply, installation and construction, testing and commissioning to operation and maintenance (“O&M”). The details of our EPC services are as follows: • Solar EPC: Our Solar EPC capabilities include solar water pumping projects, Ground-mounted solar PV projects, Grid-connected rooftop solar PV projects, and agriculture feeder solarisation. We undertake central government funded EPC projects for state government entities, government undertakings and power utilities with applications across agricultural and other public infrastructure requirements, including projects aligned with the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan (“PM-KUSUM”) Scheme. We are currently executing 7 Solar EPC projects comprising of 38.01% of our EPC Order Book. • Electrical EPC: Our Electrical EPC business comprises of turnkey execution of electrical infrastructure projects, including substations, transmission and distribution infrastructure, distribution lines, distribution transformers, rural electrification and associated electrical works. Our capabilities include the construction of LV/MV distribution lines and 33/11 kV substations, installation of distribution transformers, household metering and end-to-end rural power solutions. We undertake design and engineering, procurement and supply of equipment and materials, civil and foundation works, erection and installation, cabling and termination, testing and commissioning and project handover for power utilities, railway infrastructure entities and central & state government entities. Power demand in the country has been on a rise in the past decade, with an exception during FY21 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Peak energy demand grew at a CAGR of 5.2% from FY21 to FY26 and is expected to grow at a CAGR of 7.9% by FY32 reaching 388 GW. Rising peak electricity demand is expected to structurally support solar capacity addition in India, as solar is one of the fastest deployable and cost-competitive sources for meeting incremental daytime demand from commercial, industrial, agricultural and cooling loads. India’s power requirement recorded a steady CAGR of 6.0% during FY21-FY26. Over the same period, the gap between electricity requirement and supply narrowed sharply, declining from 5 BU in FY21 to nearly 0 BU in FY26, reflecting a significant improvement in supply adequacy and system reliability. Rapid capacity addition, especially in renewable energy and steady growth in thermal power improved overall power availability. (Source: CARE Report) 357 As per the National Electricity Plan (NEP), India’s installed power capacity is projected to increase to 900 GW by FY32, requiring significant investments across the generation sector. During FY27-FY32, total generation investments are estimated at Rs 22.9 lakh crore, with renewables accounting for ~87% of the planned investments. Solar is expected to attract the highest investment of around Rs 9.0 lakh crore, followed by wind of Rs 3.8 lakh crore and BESS around Rs 3.49 lakh crore. In comparison, investments in conventional power are projected at Rs 2.9 lakh crore. The projected investment pipeline highlights India's increasing focus on renewable energy, storage and grid-balancing infrastructure to support future power demand growth and decarbonisation goals. SIGNIFICANT FACTORS AFFECTING OUR RESULTS OF OPERATIONS AND FINANCIAL CONDITION Our business, prospects, results of operations and financial conditions are affected by a number of factors, including the following: Project execution and timely completion Our ability to complete our projects within the expected completion dates or at all is subject to a number of risks and unforeseen events, including, without limitation collaboration with third parties, changes in applicable regulations, availability of adequate financing arrangements on commercially viable terms, as well as an inability or delay in securing necessary statutory or regulatory approvals for such projects. Our EPC projects are required to achieve commercial operation no later than the scheduled commercial operation dates specified under the relevant EPC contracts, or by the end of the extension period, if any is granted by our clients. We provide our clients with performance guarantees for completion of the construction of our projects within a specified time frame. The client may also be entitled to terminate the EPC contract in the event of delay in completion of the work if the delay is not on account of any of the agreed exceptions. In addition to the risk of termination by the client, delays in completion of development may result in cost overruns, lower or no returns on capital and reduced revenue for the client thus impacting the project’s performance, as well as failure to meet scheduled debt service payment dates and increased interest costs from our financing agreements for the projects. Delay in completion of projects have major repercussions on our business including but not limited to fines and penalties payable to the vendor as per the agreed terms and conditions, partial forfeiture of our earnest money and we may be subject to disputes brought by the vendors or suppliers, etc. Our MIS framework enhances monitoring of receivables, project timelines, and resource utilisation, enabling management to make real-time, data-driven decisions. As of August 31, 2026, our EPC Order Book stood at ₹65,171 lakhs, representing 3.04 times our revenue from the EPC segment in Fiscal 2026. This underpins our growth trajectory but remains subject to risks of cancellation, delay, or slower execution. Government policies, public spending and scheme-led demand A significant portion of our EPC revenue is derived from projects awarded by central and state government entities, government undertakings, state power utilities and renewable energy agencies, which are largely funded under central government programmes such as the PM-KUSUM Scheme, the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme and the Jal Jeevan Mission. Our EPC segment accounted for 70.42%, 53.09% and 57.43% of our revenue from operations in Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, respectively. Accordingly, our results of operations depend significantly on budgetary allocations, the timely release of funds and the continuation, extension or modification of such schemes. According to the Care Report, the PM-KUSUM Scheme has been extended up to March 31, 2027, Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 has been extended up to December 2028 with an outlay of ₹8.69 trillion, an extension of RDSS up to FY28 is being sought, and public capital expenditure has increased from ₹2 lakh crore in FY15 to a budget estimate of ₹12.2 lakh crore in FY27. Any reduction in government spending, delay in tender issuance or change in the policy framework applicable to these schemes could affect our order inflows and revenue. For further details, see “Risk Factors-Our revenues from our EPC business are dependent on our ability to continuously identify and secure new projects and maintain relationships with our existing customers. Any 360 inability to secure new projects, reduction or cancellation of orders, or deterioration in our relationships with our customers may adversely affect our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows” on page 28. Order Book, ability to secure new projects and competitive bidding Our revenue from EPC projects depends on our ability to identify, bid for and secure new projects, which are generally awarded through competitive tendering on the basis of technical and financial qualification criteria followed by price bids, including reverse auctions. As of August 31, 2026, our EPC Order Book stood at ₹65,171 lakhs, diversified across Solar EPC (37.93%), Electrical EPC (28.08%) and Water EPC (33.99%), which reduces our dependence on any single project category. However, our Order Book is not necessarily indicative of future revenue, as projects may be delayed, modified, curtailed or cancelled. We face competition from established EPC contractors, cable manufacturers and integrated infrastructure companies, some of which have greater scale, financial resources and longer track records, and aggressive bidding may put pressure on our margins. See “Risk Factors- Our Order Book may not be representative of our future results and our actual income may be significantly less than the estimates reflected in our Order Book. The products that are included in our Order Book may be delayed, modified, cancelled not fully paid, or suspended by our customers and, therefore our Order Book is not necessarily indicative of our future revenue or profit. Any inability to realise the value of our products could have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operation and financial condition” and “Risk Factors – We face competitive pressures from the existing competitors and new entrants in both public and private sector. Increased competition and aggressive bidding by such competitors are expected to make our ability to procure business in future more uncertain which may adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations” on pages 33 and 39, respectively. Timing of project execution, revenue recognition and vertical mix Revenue from our EPC contracts is recognised over time based on the progress of work performed, and is therefore dependent on the stage of execution of projects during a period, the timing of new project awards, receipt of site clearances and approvals and achievement of contractual milestones. As a result, revenue from our individual EPC verticals has fluctuated significantly between periods. Revenue from Water EPC was ₹11,332.39 lakhs (55.55% of revenue from operations) in Fiscal 2024, ₹4,701.90 lakhs (16.65%) in Fiscal 2025 and ₹9,237.39 lakhs (30.38%) in Fiscal 2026, while revenue from Solar EPC increased from ₹361.06 lakhs (1.77%) in Fiscal 2024 to ₹7,269.80 lakhs (23.91%) in Fiscal 2026, and revenue from Electrical EPC increased from ₹23.09 lakhs (0.11%) in Fiscal 2024 to ₹6,018.77 lakhs (21.31%) in Fiscal 2025 before decreasing to ₹4,906.91 lakhs (16.14%) in Fiscal 2026. Our solar projects also depend on our customers’ ability to acquire land, obtain site approvals and arrange grid connectivity. Delays in completion may expose us to liquidated damages (₹16.90 lakhs in Fiscal 2026), cost overruns and invocation of performance guarantees. Accordingly, our historical results may not be indicative of our future performance. See “Risk Factors – Our revenue from operations is subject to significant fluctuation from period to period, and historical financial performance may not be indicative of future results” on page 36. Customer concentration We derive a significant portion of our revenue from a limited number of customers. Customers individually contributing more than 10% of our revenue from operations together accounted for ₹13,080.61 lakhs (43.02%), ₹16,013.07 lakhs (56.70%) and ₹11,232.38 lakhs (55.06%) of our revenue from operations in Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, respectively, and our largest customer accounted for 29.21%, 17.52% and 55.06% of our revenue from operations in these periods. The composition of our top customers varies from year to year depending on the timing, nature and value of projects awarded, and the loss of, or a significant reduction in business from, any of these customers could adversely affect our results of operations. See “Risk Factors – A substantial portion of our revenues is dependent on our top 10 customers. As of the Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, we derived 81.81 %, 87.57 % and 88.68% respectively, of our revenue from our top 10 customers. The concentration of our revenue from such top 10 customers exposes us to greater risks if these projects are delayed or cancelled. Any such material delay or cancellation of the project may have a material adverse effect on our financial condition, results of operations and cash flows” on page 23. Cost and availability of raw materials, components and equipment Our principal raw materials in the Manufacturing segment are aluminium and copper rods, PVC and XLPE compounds and galvanised steel wires, while our EPC projects require solar PV modules, inverters, module mounting structures, transformers, switchgear, pumps, pipes, cables and other balance-of-system equipment, which we procure from third-party suppliers. Cost of materials consumed (including erection and site expenses) 361 together with changes in inventories accounted for 69.53%, 70.34% and 72.77% of our revenue from operations in Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, respectively. Prices of copper, aluminium and PVC are volatile and linked to global commodity markets and, according to the Care Report, the competitive nature of the market often makes it difficult to transfer such cost increases to end-users. Further, where our contracts are awarded on a fixed-price basis without adequate price variation provisions, increases in the cost of materials and equipment after submission of bids may not be recoverable and could reduce our margins. Any disruption in the timely supply of materials may also delay project execution. See “Risk Factors – Our business and profitability are significantly dependent on the availability and cost of finished and raw materials, components and equipment required for our EPC Projects and Manufacturing Business. We rely on third-party suppliers to meet these requirements. Any disruption in the timely and adequate supply of such materials, components and equipment, or any volatility in their prices, may have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations and financial condition” on page 27. Working capital requirements and timely collection of receivables Our EPC business is working capital intensive, as we incur expenditure towards procurement, mobilisation, manpower and the furnishing of bank guarantees before receiving milestone-linked payments, which are subject to inspection, certification and release of funds by our customers. Our trade receivables increased from ₹3,718.57 lakhs as at March 31, 2024 to ₹6,752.60 lakhs as at March 31, 2025 and ₹15,274.05 lakhs as at March 31, 2026, and our trade receivable days (trade receivables as at the end of the year divided by revenue from operations, multiplied by 365) were 183, 87 and 67 days for Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, respectively. Our Net Working Capital Days were 225.51, 124.57 and 80.45 in Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, respectively, and we had net cash used in operating activities of ₹4,694.95 lakhs in Fiscal 2026. According to the Care Report, outstanding dues of distribution companies have declined to ₹17,744 crore as of August 2026 from ₹78,000 crore as of March 2024; however, any delay in payments by government entities, DISCOMs or other customers could adversely affect our cash flows. A portion of the Net Proceeds is proposed to be utilised towards funding our working capital requirements. See “Objects of the Offer” on page 113. Access to and cost of financing, including bank guarantee facilities We fund our working capital requirements primarily through internal accruals and borrowings, including cash credit and working capital demand loans, term loans and unsecured loans. Our total borrowings increased from ₹5,889.09 lakhs as at March 31, 2024 to ₹15,661.62 lakhs as at March 31, 2026, and our finance costs increased from ₹922.07 lakhs in Fiscal 2024 to ₹2,273.18 lakhs in Fiscal 2026, representing 4.52% and 7.48% of our revenue from operations, respectively. Our EPC contracts also require us to furnish bid security, performance and advance payment bank guarantees, for which we provide margin money; bank balances other than cash and cash equivalents of ₹2,792.97 lakhs as at March 31, 2026 are held as security against bank guarantees, letters of credit and borrowings. Our ability to bid for and execute projects therefore depends on our ability to obtain adequate fund-based and non-fund-based limits on commercially acceptable terms, and changes in interest rates, which are largely floating and linked to external benchmarks, affect our finance costs. See “Risk Factors-We are required to furnish bank guarantees as part of our business. Our inability to arrange such guarantees or the invocation of such guarantees or our inability to fulfil any or all of the obligations under such bank guarantees may or may not adversely affect our cash flows and financial condition” on page 40. Segment mix and demand for Cables and Conductors Our Manufacturing segment supplies LT Cables and Conductors primarily to power utilities, EPC contractors and institutional customers, and its performance depends on order inflows from distribution and transmission projects, raw material prices and competition from organised and unorganised players. Revenue from our Manufacturing segment was ₹8,666.00 lakhs, ₹13,159.15 lakhs and ₹8,917.91 lakhs in Fiscals 2024, 2025 and 2026, respectively. As our EPC and Manufacturing businesses have different margin profiles, working capital cycles and cost structures, changes in the relative contribution of each segment affect our overall margins. According to the Care Report, demand for conductors is linked to the expansion and modernisation of transmission and distribution infrastructure and distribution-system strengthening, and India’s transmission network is expected to add approximately 40,000 circuit kilometres of inter-state and 27,500 circuit kilometres of intra-state transmission lines under ongoing projects. Weather, seasonality and site conditions Our EPC operations are carried out at project sites and are affected by weather conditions, including heavy rainfall during the monsoon, cyclones and extreme temperatures, which may restrict site access, civil works and 362 installation activities, and by site-specific conditions such as land availability, right of way and grid connectivity. Such factors may cause variations in our execution progress and revenue between quarters and periods. Taxation, regulatory proceedings and contingent liabilities Changes in tax laws, the availability of tax benefits and the outcome of tax proceedings may affect our results of operations. MATERIAL ACCOUNTING POLICIES 2.1 Basis of preparation 365 (i) Compliance with Ind AS The Restated Financial Information comprises the Restated Statement of Assets and Liabilities of the Group as at March 31, 2026, March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2024, the related Restated Statement of Profit and Loss (including Other Comprehensive Income), the Restated Statement of Cash Flows and the Restated Statement of Changes in Equity for each of the years ended March 31, 2026, March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2024, and the Statement of Material Accounting Policies and explanatory notes, collectively referred to as the “Restated Financial Information”. These Restated Financial Information have been prepared by the Management of the Company for the purpose of inclusion in the Draft Red Herring Prospectus (“DRHP”) to be filed with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (“SEBI”) in connection with the proposed initial public offering of equity shares of the Company (the “Offer”). These Restated Financial Information have been prepared by the Company to comply, in all material respects, with the requirements of: a) Section 26 of Part I of Chapter III of the Companies Act, 2013 (the “Act”); b) the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018, as amended (“ICDR Regulations”); and c) the Guidance Note on Reports in Company Prospectuses (Revised 2019) issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (“ICAI”), as amended (the “Guidance Note”). These Restated Financial Information have been compiled by the Management from: a) Audited Special Purpose Consolidated Ind AS Financial Statements of the Group as at and for the year ended March 31, 2026, which were prepared in accordance with the Indian Accounting Standards (“Ind AS”), as prescribed under Section 133 of the Act read with the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, as amended, and other accounting principles generally accepted in India. These Special Purpose Consolidated Ind AS Financial Statements were prepared based on the audited statutory financial statements of the Group for the year ended March 31, 2026, which were originally prepared in accordance with the accounting principles generally accepted in India applicable to the Group (“IGAAP”), after giving effect to adjustments required for compliance with Ind AS, and were approved by the Board of Directors at their meeting held on September 28, 2026. b) Audited Special Purpose Consolidated Ind AS Financial Statements of the Group as at and for the year ended March 31, 2025, together with the comparative financial information as at and for the year ended March 31, 2024, which were prepared in accordance with Ind AS, as prescribed under Section 133 of the Act read with the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, as amended, and other accounting principles generally accepted in India. These Special Purpose Consolidated Ind AS Financial Statements were prepared based on the respective audited statutory financial statements originally prepared in accordance with IGAAP, after giving effect to adjustments required for compliance with Ind AS, and were approved by the Board of Directors at their meeting held on September 28, 2026. The accounting policies have been consistently applied by the Group in the preparation of the Restated Financial Information and are consistent with those adopted in the preparation of the Audited Special Purpose Consolidated Ind AS Financial Statements for the year ended March 31, 2026. These Restated Financial Information have been prepared by the Group on the basis that it will continue to operate as a going concern. (ii) Historical cost convention The Restated Financial Information have been prepared on an accrual basis under historical cost convention except for certain assets and liabilities that are measured at fair values at the end of each reporting period, as explained in the respective accounting policies described in subsequent paragraphs. Historical cost is generally based on the fair value of the consideration given in exchange for goods and services. Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date, regardless of whether that price is directly observable or estimated using another valuation technique. In estimating the fair value of an asset or a liability, the Group takes into account the characteristics of the asset or liability if market participants would take those characteristics into account when pricing the asset or liability at the measurement date. Fair value for measurement and/ or disclosure 366 purposes in the Restated Financial Information is determined on such a basis, except for leasing transactions that are within the scope of Ind AS 116 Leases (see paragraph (d) below) and measurements that have some similarities to fair value but are not fair value, such as net realisable value in Ind AS 2 Inventories or value in use in Ind AS 36 Impairment of Assets (see paragraph (f) below). (iii) Classification of assets and liabilities into current/non-current All assets and liabilities have been classified as current or non-current as per the Group’s normal operating cycle and other criteria set out in Schedule III to the Act. The operating cycle of the Group is the time between the acquisition of assets for processing and their realisation in cash or cash equivalents. (iv) Business combination under common control Business combinations involving entities or businesses under common control are accounted for using the pooling of interest method. Under pooling of interest method, the assets and liabilities of the combining entities or businesses are reflected at their carrying amounts after making adjustments necessary to harmonise the accounting policies. The financial information in the Restated Financial Information in respect of prior periods is restated as if the business combination had occurred from the beginning of the preceding period in the Restated Financial Information, irrespective of the actual date of the combination. However, if business combination occurs after that date, the prior period information is restated only from that date. The identity of the reserves is preserved in the same form in which they appeared in the Restated Financial Information and the difference, if any, between the amount recorded as share capital issued plus any additional consideration in the form of cash or other assets and the amount of share capital of the transferor is transferred to capital reserve. (v) Statement of cash flows Cash flows are reported using the indirect method, whereby profit/loss before tax is adjusted for the effects of transactions of a non-cash nature, any deferrals or accruals of past or future operating cash receipts or payments and items of income or expense associated with investing or financing activities. The cash flows from operating, investing and financing activities of the Group are segregated. (vi) Rounding off The Restated Financial Information are presented in Indian rupee (₹), which is the Group’s functional and presentation currency unless stated otherwise. All amounts have been rounded off to the nearest ₹ lakhs, up to two decimals. Value “0.00” or “(0.00)” represents an amount which is below the rounding off threshold.
